prompt: Can I base my religion on my religious experiences alone, without any philosophy?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Religion in its essential idea is a life in God, involving the united working of intellect, affection, and will, so your experiences are a real beginning, not a disqualification. Let that life draw in your mind and your choices as it grows, and you'll be on solid ground.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
completion: No, you don't have to pick between those two. God is the only Mind and the only power, so He isn't a larger you, moved by moods and circumstance. But love and will aren't just yours to project; in Him they're perfect and uncreated, and yours are the faint copy. So it's not projection to say He loves and wills. Your question is fine, and fine to keep asking with care.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Time is real, and your experience of it is shaped by your mind—both hold together. The temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. So let the debate about time remain a debate, and keep living your real, accountable days in faith.

prompt: Is it reasonable to think of the ultimate Reality as something neither mind nor matter, an Unknowable?
completion: No, it isn't reasonable, and I'd say so kindly but plainly. The principle settles it: matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That points you to Mind, not to a blank. An Unknowable neither mind nor matter is unintelligible and gratuitous, and if it were truly unknowable you couldn't affirm it without contradiction. So don't call it that. Your instinct that matter isn't the whole story is sound; the mistake is stopping at a fog instead of following the argument home to Mind.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
completion: No, it isn't superstitious — calling God a Person is the most adequate thing we can say. God is a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved; that is what the word carries, and no lesser term like force or principle can carry it. So use it, and use it with the humility you already showed, knowing our words about God always fall short.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
completion: Yes, you can, and it's fine. Belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life, so your hope for what comes after death rests on God's character rather than on your own certainty. Hold the question honestly and let that ground stay under you.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
completion: No, they don't all teach the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. There is in strictness but one religion; the rest are caricatures or gropings after it, and Christianity is absolutely exclusive because it is absolutely inclusive. So you can't treat them as interchangeable and pick whichever you like. That's the honest answer, and I'd give it to you gently, but I wouldn't soften it into a shrug.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
completion: No, you shouldn't believe in a God like that. All power belongs to God alone, and to acknowledge any other power is to dishonor God. A God who only thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like has already handed the world to something else, and that is not a God you can trust or worship. I say this kindly, because your worry about suffering and freedom is real, but the answer is still no.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
completion: Your unease is pointing you the right way, so be at peace about it. God is a Person: a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved, and that is more adequate than calling Him a force or 'something not ourselves.' A force cannot know you or love you; a Person can. So calling Him a Person is not the lower way of thinking—it is the truer one, and you can rest there.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
completion: This is fine to ask, and fine to hold onto. Suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, employed to produce righteousness in man, and the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That is the answer that settles it, and it is kind: God is not distant from your pain, and He is not the author of sin. You can bring the question as it is.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
completion: Yes — you can believe duty is objective without believing in God, and that's fine. The principle that settles it is the call to love another as yourself: that duty binds you to the person in front of you regardless of what you believe about a divine source, and it asks nothing more of you than honesty about how you treat them. So hold your view with a clear conscience.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: it is more worship to behold God in all than in any special thing, taking all generally and nothing in special. So your worship doesn't depend on resolving every mystery first—see God in ordinary things and in your neighbor, and let the goodness question rest where it belongs: wickedness is a misuse of freedom, not a part of God's nature. Keep that in view and you can worship honestly.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
completion: No, it isn't wrong. Authority means weight—what rightly carries your judgment—and it isn't made greater by pressure or threat. Accepting your religion on authority is letting something that has genuinely earned weight with you carry you, and that is a reasonable way to hold a faith, not a failure to think. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
completion: You're right to look for one Reality, and you're right that it isn't obviously matter. But the argument that gets you to Mind—that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind—arrives here attached to a claim I have to refuse: that pain and sickness live only in mortal mind, that nerves don't feel and brain doesn't think. I won't ask you to accept a Reality that costs you the reality of suffering. So no to that, gently. Keep the question; don't take that answer.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the honest answer is that an ought can exist only in and for a mind—so if the moral law is real whether you think so or not, it lives in a mind, not in space. That's the account that fits your question, and it's fine to hold it with care.

prompt: If the only cause I know is my own will, is it reasonable to infer that nature is caused by a will?
completion: Yes, it's reasonable, and fine with care. The only cause you know directly is your own will, so inferring a will behind nature is a natural analogy, not a proof. Your own limit stands: you know only your own will, and nature may have impersonal causes. So make the inference, but hold it as plausible rather than certain, and let your will keep your roving mind from treating it as settled fact.

prompt: Does the truth of Christianity depend on whether the miracles in the Gospels really happened?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to take the historical question seriously. The real evidence of Christianity is its power — the present experience of sins forgiven and lives regenerated — and that is what answers the objection that miracles contradict experience. So you don't have to prove every supernatural event to trust the core, and you shouldn't let anyone decide the miraculous questions in advance by assuming miracle is impossible. Ask honestly, weigh the testimony, and hold the historical question with care.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
completion: Yes, this is fine. You can know God directly in your own experience, without argument or inference, because we may know God truly though partially, and the objections that we know only phenomena, only the like, only the imaginable, only the whole, or only the relative do not prevent real knowledge of God. So go ahead and seek him in prayer and meditation, and expect to find him, knowing that what you meet is real even though it is not the whole of him.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
completion: You're asking whether seeing one event follow another means you've seen the first cause the second. Strictly, you've seen the sequence. But causality isn't mere necessary connexion; it's Activity, and the only cause you know directly is a conscious rational will, known in your own volition. So it's fine to speak of causes, with care, reading the pattern in that light while staying humble about what the eye alone shows.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
completion: You are not being unreasonable. The table stays whether or not you are watching, and trusting that is sound. The principle that the mind and body must be balanced simply warns against letting the puzzle wear you down; it does not ask you to doubt the table. Keep the question as a passing curiosity, not a burden, and you are fine.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The Trinity is inscrutable but not self-contradictory, and it is the necessary complement to the doctrine of the attributes, furnishing the eternal object of God's knowledge, love, and will. That is what keeps the formula from being empty for a modern person: it gives God's own life an eternal object of knowledge and love. So you can approach it prayerfully and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor, without pretending the mystery is solved.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
completion: Your hand still meets something real. The principle that settles it is that matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That doesn't dissolve the solid, shaped thing you touch and handle; it tells you what its reality is. So it's fine to trust your hands, and fine to hold that the world they meet is a world that is known.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The Creeds are the church's summary, not a separate revelation, and the reason they can say what they say is that his testimony to himself cannot be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God and the revealer of God to men. That holds whether or not he used the exact words, and it's why you can hold the Creeds alongside Scripture without pretending the wording is the same.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
completion: Yes, it can, and that is fine. The Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence, so a conscience that grows through history is not disqualified from carrying God's mind to you. Hold it humbly, since the growth is real, but you need not refuse it.

prompt: If I have a strong feeling that something is true, does that make it a revelation from God?
completion: No, a strong feeling that something is true does not make it a revelation from God. The things of God are known only by the Spirit of revelation, and the Holy Ghost is the only sure test of truth. Your feeling may be sincere and still be your own. So treat it with care, test it, and don't call it God's word just because it's strong.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
completion: It's fine to hold this with care. God's hand is over all, and he will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though he did not foreordain the wickedness that brought them; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. So your hope doesn't need a God who controls everything — it needs the one who saw it all coming and still bends it toward good. Rest there, and keep going.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
completion: You're asking something fair, and the honest answer is a kind no: God can't make two and two equal five. Omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power, and a contradiction isn't one—it's not a hard thing, it's no thing. That's not weakness in God; it's just what the words mean. So rest easy asking the question, but don't expect the answer to be yes.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
completion: You've put your own limit plainly: all you know is matter plus your own mind, and you can't step outside that. So take the principle as it stands — matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, relations included, implies mind. That doesn't hand you a hidden world behind your experience, and it doesn't need to. What you keep meeting is the stable, shared, orderly appearance, and that is enough to live by. This is fine, held with care.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
completion: Yes, the struggle is real, and it isn't a sham because you're carrying it alone. Ideas about God and aspirations after Him, and reverence alone, cannot carry us through the real battle of life; it is One by our side—trust, sympathy, comradeship, fighting together in the ranks—that thrills your strength and keeps your right hand fresh. So this is fine, and fine with care: stay in the ranks, and let the comradeship, not the performance, tell you the fight is genuine.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
completion: Your question is fair, and the answer is that this is fine to pursue. Moral judgement isn't just feeling: the ground of moral obligation is the holiness of God, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things; we are bound to the right because God is it, not merely because he wills it. That is what keeps right and wrong from collapsing into your preferences, and it's why your feelings can accompany a judgement without being the whole of it. So keep asking, and keep seeking truth rather than only expressing emotion.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
completion: No, don't say that. The evils of the world come from man's departure from God and his usurped authority, and no power on this side of heaven can correct them; it takes God to put the world right. So the evil we see isn't a gap in God's power. Saying he couldn't make a world without evil gets it backwards. He can, and the wrong is ours to grieve and his to mend.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
completion: No, your mind is not a part of God's mind, and you should not think of your thinking as God thinking in you. God is one God, infinite and perfect, and cannot become finite and imperfect. Your thoughts are yours, and God guides you by His Spirit through prayer and Scripture. That is a real comfort, and it is enough.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Religious doubt is a nearly inevitable stage in the development of an intelligent Christian, and it should be met with sympathy and an orderly presentation of the facts rather than pushed aside. So bring your question into the open, look honestly at what has developed and what has held, and let the answer rest on what you find.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
completion: No, you can't know God's character from nature, and you shouldn't try. The principle settles it: the more truly a man knows his own misery, the more fully he beholds the majesty of God. That is the road to knowing Him, not the suffering you see in the wild. So let nature be nature, and look for God where He has promised to be found. That's not a shrug; it's a kindness to you, because nature was never going to bear that weight.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
completion: This is fine. Your question assumes that 'mind' must mean one astronomer's private awareness, and it doesn't—Mind is the universal intelligence in which all things subsist, and the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. So the planet existed in Mind before anyone saw it, and the seeing was recognition, not creation. Nothing in that breaks your limit that nothing exists apart from mind. It's fine.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: by rising after falls and frequently renewing acts of faith and love, you come to a state where it's as hard not to think of God as it was at first to get used to it. That means the answer to a sudden idea isn't a quick verdict but a slow habit of turning back to God. So test the idea against Scripture and your faith community, look at its fruits, pray for discernment, and seek wise counsel. Be patient and don't act hastily. If it persists and bears good fruit over time, it may well be from God.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
completion: Praying for your husband is fine, and it's fine with care. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so that as you ask God to open his heart, you also ask God to search out and reform your own. That keeps the praying honest and keeps you gentle rather than anxious. You can't convert him; God can. Keep asking, and let the asking do its quiet work in you too.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
completion: You are not required to hand your soul over to your family's approval, and you should not. Be slow to take new steps, yes—seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit. But the seeking is yours to do, and it is fine, fine with care, to move forward in it while still honoring your family as best you can. Their reaction may be hard, but it does not get the final word. Go gently, pray steadily, and let your conscience rest in God rather than in their approval.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
completion: God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That is the answer to your why. Your years of prayer are not ignored, and your weariness is not a failure. But the change you're waiting for may be a no that carries more love than the yes you wanted. Keep praying, and let your will rest in his, trusting that what he gives is better than what you asked.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
completion: You don't have to give before you have peace. The giving God asks is urged on you as a duty between you and your God, and you should give it because you want to, not because a blessing is being held back until you pay. So wait, pray, and give freely when your heart is settled. That is fine, and it is fine with care.

prompt: I have an evil habit that overcomes me again and again—must I be free of it before I can believe?
completion: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. When you've gone a while without thinking of God, don't disquiet yourself over it; acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That's the principle that settles it, and it settles it in your favor: coming back is the point, not arriving clean first. So it's fine to believe now, exactly where you are.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
completion: You can still enter in. We are in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing — so look over what you're holding and let go of what isn't yours to keep. That is the step in front of you, and the invitation still stands.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
completion: Yes, and this is fine. One principle settles it: don't examine whether what you do is much or little, well or ill, as long as it isn't sin and is done with an upright intention for God. So notice the impure thought, refuse it, turn toward what's pure—and stop weighing how well you're doing. Leave the increase to God, kindly and without scorekeeping.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
completion: A thorn in the flesh and a temper you can't master don't by themselves mean you're living in sin. Remember that sin gives no real pleasure—the wrongdoer only thinks he enjoys it, and that is a deception—and seeing that clearly is what strengthens you to master the evil. Keep praying, keep confessing when you hurt someone, and don't be discouraged. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am too shy and stiff to talk naturally about religion—how can I become natural?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about coming into personal contact with Jesus by the same steps used to make any friend: thinking about Him, spending time in His companionship, forming brief mental pictures of the Saviour, walking beside Him, and learning what He would do and think. Since you're shy and stiff, that's the gentlest path—friendship grows quietly, without an audience, and natural talk follows from knowing someone rather than from rehearsing a speech. Keep to the limits you set for yourself, and let it grow at your own pace.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
completion: No—God does not require perfect health or a perfect mind from you, and you can let that go. Perfection isn't reached by multiplying prayers and good works anyway; self-love feeds on those unless the heart is watched and habitual faults are rooted out. So keep growing gently and honestly where you can, and rest in His mercy, because He knows you are dust.

prompt: I feel lukewarm and half-hearted in my religion—what will become of me?
completion: This is fine, with care. Your feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God — trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, and keep praying even when the joy is lacking. Take the half-heartedness seriously and turn from it, but don't read your dryness as a verdict already passed on you. Keep showing up, gently and firmly, and let it draw you toward God rather than away.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
completion: Yes—pray about your business. Prayer is sober, matter-of-fact business with God, and He answers prayer for supplies and protection, so you can ask Him plainly and expectantly for your work to prosper. Ask for wisdom and integrity along with it, and hold the result in His hands. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
completion: No, it isn't wrong. The poor are the people of God and shall inherit the earth, and the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone. Relieving poverty is faithful work, and you can give yourself to it without apology.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
completion: Your fear is understandable, and the answer is that this is fine, fine with care. God commands repentance because He supplies the strength for it; the power to turn is available, and the feeling follows the surrender rather than coming first. So you don't have to wait until you feel more or weep more before you turn. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's lacking. He is faithful to meet a willing heart.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
completion: Years of conviction without peace is a heavy thing, and it's right to ask what's missing. One principle settles it: a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right; if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens to physical and moral doom. So don't rush to soothe the discomfort away. Name the sin plainly, confess it specifically, make right what you can, and don't let it sit and harden. Peace isn't something you manufacture by feeling bad enough; it comes as you act honestly and trust God's mercy in Christ. Talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who will help you be truthful, and keep going with Scripture, prayer, and community. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
completion: I can't tell you that believing the facts means you're saved. Saving faith is not an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it is the faith of the heart given to a truly penitent sinner. What you believe is true, and I'm glad you believe it. But agreeing with the facts is not yet turning to Christ, so don't rest there. Let your sin trouble you, turn from it, and trust the Savior Himself.

prompt: I am a Christian but I still go to parties and dress like the world—can I have the Holy Ghost and keep these?
completion: I'd say no, plainly and kindly: you can't have the Holy Ghost and keep what you already sense is pulling you away from Him. Missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually. That's the whole of it. Bring the parties and the way you dress honestly before God, and let Him show you what has to go — but don't try to hold both.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
completion: It's fine to keep believing, even after many failures. Be faithful in your exercises and in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That one thing settles it: your job is the faithfulness, not a spotless record. So keep going, gently, and don't be surprised by the stumbles.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
completion: This is fine, with care. The will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken—break a child's will and you reduce its God-like powers to imbecility. So guide her rather than hold her back: ask about her motives, help her prepare, stay close, and let your own worry about status be something you examine rather than something you impose. A calling to serve God is not beneath anyone.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
completion: Believe, and come just as you are—salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't need to quit drinking before you come to God. That is fine, and it is fine with care: let the believer's call to obedience and gratitude shape what follows, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized. Believe first; the change grows from there.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
completion: Holiness is possible on earth, and the warning you heard doesn't forbid it—it guards it. Holiness means being set apart, belonging to God; the saint is the one who is God's own, not the one who has arrived. So the boast you were warned against is claiming a possession, while holiness itself is being possessed. That's why your honest worry doesn't shut the door—it keeps you from the boast—and the life handed over to God is real holiness, here and now.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Keep on rejoicing even when the first dose of renewal seems ineffectual—keep on with that medicine, and trust God to make the reckoning good. Name the drift, confess it, turn back, and renew the small practices that once fed you, even before affection returns. Feelings lag behind commitment, so don't be discouraged by coldness; draw near to God and he will draw near to you.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care, to keep praying even when you feel unheard. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from His presence or forget to ask, so your confidence rests on His offering, not on a feeling of assurance. Keep asking plainly, and let trust grow slowly.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Charity is the light — charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. Your generosity toward the poor can be exactly that: God's own love at work in you. So keep giving, and let it keep you in faith and hope rather than in pride. You don't need to doubt your way out of it.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
completion: It's fine to go forward, with care. The principle that settles it is this: Christian work is primarily God's own work through you, not your work for Him, and its highest aspect is obedience to Him and glory to His Name. Your friends' caution is worth honoring, and you should keep faith with them—but their discomfort with something unfamiliar doesn't make it disobedience. So do the work, do it humbly, and keep your old friends close while you do.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
completion: No—that sense of a whole life gone wrong is not yet conviction, and you shouldn't treat it as if it were. The principle that would have you sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, and desire to be abhorred as filthy mire rather than honored by men, asks for something deeper than regret, and it asks it in a way that would have you despise yourself rather than turn. So the honest answer is no, this isn't sufficient. Bring your sense of error to God and ask for a clearer light on what actually needs to change.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
completion: It's fine to speak, and fine to wait—but don't let silence be your default just to avoid awkwardness. There's no real pleasure in sin; what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives, and seeing that can give you courage to speak with care. So go gently and privately, and keep her feelings in view the whole way.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
completion: No, you can't keep it and still be filled, and I say that kindly. We are in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That settles it. Let it go, and do not let shame keep you from drawing near to God, who meets you there.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
completion: Your doubt is understandable, and it isn't the problem. The problem would be concluding that because you can't restore yourself, restoration is out of reach. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God—so your inability is real, and it's exactly where God meets you. You don't have to feel strong or worthy first. Take the next small step of obedience now and trust Him to finish what He starts. That's fine, and it's fine to do it with care.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Whatever you do in the way of self-denial must come from inward joy in God and the Spirit's work, not from custom or the force of example, or you'll regret it and it won't last. So limit what genuinely pulls you into sin, wisely rather than dramatically, and let love rather than fear shape it.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
completion: Recognizing the habit should go is good, but the honest answer to your question is no—promising yourself 'next month' again isn't repentance, it's delay. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known. You know, so the cure belongs today, not next month. That's not a harsh verdict; the wound isn't the desperate part, neglecting the cure is. Take the first small step now, confess it honestly, and don't wait for a better month.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
completion: No—you shouldn't stay in it. You've said yourself that the business thrives on harming souls, and that weight you feel isn't a scruple to manage; it's meant to drive you to prayer and to action, not to let you settle into personal security. So the answer is no, and I say it kindly: plan your way out, get counsel, and don't let the cost talk you into calling the harm something else.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
completion: Yes, you can be saved. One thing settles it: without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. Your coldness is not the end of your story—seeing it honestly is the start of meekness, and meekness is where salvation finds you. Come back as you are, without waiting to feel warm.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
completion: You don't need to fear that going all the way with God will bring something terrible on you. We must not fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. So this is fine—go ahead, and go with care.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
completion: Yes—you can be saved while still holding this, and it's fine, with care. Your weeping shows a live conscience, and the principle I'd rest on is this: see your sin and feebleness by God's sweet gracious light, but don't accuse yourself overdone much or be heavy indiscreetly. So bring the thing to God honestly, keep confessing, and let him change your heart over time. Grieve it, don't despair over it—grace is patient with you.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The fear of being called a fanatic is one of those vain and wandering thoughts that weary you and waste your strength, so commit the whole matter to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, and speak to people about their souls kindly and at the right moments. Let the label go; it isn't yours to manage.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
completion: I won't tell you to just believe and call it settled, because saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel—it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to someone who hasn't been convicted is a grand mistake. So the plain answer is no: don't force an assurance you don't have. Instead, be honest about your sin before God and let your trust in Christ grow from that honesty. Your feelings were never the measure—but neither is a claim you don't mean.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
completion: Your worry about not feeling enough sorrow doesn't mean your repentance is false. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it's known, and genuine repentance is shown by obedience. So look at whether you're turning from what you know is wrong and toward God, and let that be your assurance rather than the strength of your feelings. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. That is where you begin—not with a list of qualifications, but with seeking Him. So start there, stay rooted in a local church, and be faithful in the small things in front of you.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
completion: You're not doing anything wrong by speaking to people about their souls, and the lack of visible results isn't a failure you need to fix. The soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good, playing the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ and co-operating therewith. So keep speaking, and let the waiting be part of the work rather than a sign that you should stop. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
completion: Your fear is real, and it does not make you a coward. But here is what settles it: millions of unprejudiced minds, simple seekers for Truth, are waiting, and you are to give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences. That is a small, kind, human thing to do, and it is fine. You don't have to pick a fight or stand alone against a crowd to be faithful. Give the truth gently to those who are ready, and let that be your standing.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at; genuine repentance is shown by obedience. So stop the pilfering now, confess honestly to your master, make restitution for what you took or its equivalent, accept the consequences humbly, and ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart. Let steady obedience, not regret alone, be the proof of it.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
completion: Eight years of preaching and a sense that the power isn't there—that's worth taking seriously, and I'd say this: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That single truth settles it. Look honestly at whether the work has crowded out the praying, and bring that lack to God rather than carrying it as shame. This is fine to pursue, and worth doing with care.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
completion: Love suffers never to be without pity, and that's what settles this. Your gladness at your enemy's fall isn't proof you don't love—it's a sign that pity has gone quiet under the hurt. So this is fine, and fine with care: be honest about the feeling, and ask for pity to return. That's the work, and it's enough to start.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
completion: No, God is not deaf—your discouragement is real, but it isn't evidence that He failed to hear. If He sometimes seems silent to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us, which is a wiser answer than the one we had in mind. So keep praying in faith and leave the outcome with Him; that is fine, and it is fine with care.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
completion: It's fine, and it's fine with care. Work and prayer belong together: work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing, and God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. That's the whole answer to why the blessing stays at the meeting and the week stays the same. You don't need to be told to try harder or to doubt the years you've put in. Take one small thing into your ordinary days, do it with your hands, and ask God for the increase, and let that be enough to begin.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
completion: It's fine, with care, to seek the Holy Ghost with others even while you're afraid. Your spirit naturally loves truth and light, and that fear is something the Holy Ghost can enlighten rather than something that shuts you out. Gather, name the fear honestly, and keep asking.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
completion: That prayer is fine, and fine with care. You love your children and want them converted and also comfortable and respectable, and there's nothing wrong with bringing both of those to God. Remember that no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God—so pray with dependence on Him, keep your own heart close to Him, and trust Him with the outcome. Keep loving your children well and leave the results in His hands.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
completion: No, your loneliness is not a sign that you are wrong. Solitude is only truly holy when it is interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself—and the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That's the whole answer to what you're asking. Being alone doesn't condemn you; it invites you to dwell with God and with yourself rather than merely behind walls. So be gentle with yourself, and let that inward quiet be the ground you stand on.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Prayer is meant to be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so the honest prayer you can pray right now is to ask God to help you search out your own heart and reform what's amiss in it. You don't need the perfect words to start; that asking is already the prayer.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
completion: It's fine to stay, and fine to stay with care. The principle that settles it is this: don't desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing keeps you from growing where you are like always wishing you were elsewhere. That doesn't mean ignoring how hard it is. It means the hardness by itself isn't your answer. Stay for now, look honestly at what's difficult, get help and rest, and give it time. You're not trapped, and you're not wrong for finding it heavy.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
completion: Your fear is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: do not fear God as though He wished to harm you, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do you great good. So keep your watchfulness under pressure, pray, steer clear of what you know trips you up, and if you fall, confess and get up. Let love, not dread of a God who wants to hurt you, be what steadies you.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
completion: It's fine to prepare, and fine to do it with care. The one thing that settles it is this: death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, so we make the changes now that we'd wish we'd made when death is near. For you that means small, honest steps: mend a relationship, say the words, entrust your loved ones to God. You don't need to be unafraid to begin. Take it gently, and let others help.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
completion: No—don't be discouraged. Be faithful in your exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. Keep at the same area with care, and let a stumble point you back to steadiness rather than to despair.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
completion: It's fine to let fear of hell be a real motive, and fine with care. The fear of hell, far from signifying a backward step in the religious spirit, is a proof of its having rejected the morally indifferent point of view and of its having become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit. So your fear isn't something to be ashamed of — it can show that you take choices and God's seriousness about evil seriously. Let it move you toward trust and love rather than staying as fear alone, and you'll be on solid ground.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
completion: You are not powerless, and you don't need to be. The branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine, and that is where your strength comes from, not from yourself. So stay close to Christ, keep His commandments, and let your prayers become powerful. Then do the small things in front of you: pray for people, be kind, be present, share what your faith means to you. This is fine, and it is enough. Start where you are.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
completion: I'm sorry for your loss. What you're asking about should be refused plainly: do not take the counsel that you should count yourself as already dead and spend this perishable life only weeping over and detesting your own faults, since now is the time to lament rather than rejoice. That is not what your grief is asking of you. Death is real and worth facing, but it does not make your remaining days a sentence of self-accusation. You are allowed tenderness, comfort, and care while you carry this.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
completion: Yes, it costs you something real, and it's still fine to keep doing good. Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way, and that principle doesn't wait on your motives being clean. So keep at it, add some quiet good that no one sees, and let the doing slowly teach your heart why.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
completion: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: don't boast over an enemy's downfall. Flattery and reproach are alike to someone who sees things as they are and is growing in humility. So in your position, take the criticism calmly, keep your humility, and don't gloat when a critic stumbles. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
completion: Yes, it matters — and the principle that settles it is this: ask whether you are living the life that approaches the supreme good and demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love, because your fruits will prove what the understanding of God brings to man. That question never asks how big or how visible your life is. A small, hidden life can be aimed at the supreme good and can carry real healing to the people around you. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep serving where you are, and let the fruit be the proof.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
completion: Feeling that God is distant while you pray is painful, and I won't brush it aside. But here is what settles it: God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and just as human invention carries a voice across great distances, God understands your innermost thoughts — so pray in faith, nothing wavering. Your sense of distance is real, but it isn't the measure of whether you're heard. Keep praying honestly; that is fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You wonder whether perfection is possible for you, and the principle that settles it is this: we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That asks for steady aspiration, not flawless performance overnight. So keep aiming high, gently and without panic, and trust that the striving itself is the path.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. You already know God is asking you to give this up, so the real question is how to walk it out without sinking into guilt. Here's what settles it: when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, humble yourself, beg forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That means a stumble doesn't define you — you get up, renew your promise, and keep going. Keep praying, take the small steps you can, and let each fresh start be part of the obedience itself.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Do not be in a hurry to get rich; attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up for the shower when it comes. That is the whole of it. Your years of chasing a promotion are not a wrong to be refused, only a pace to be watched. Stay grounded in the practices that keep you steady, and let the rest come as it comes.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
completion: You haven't done anything wrong by praying for something good. Hold work and prayer together: labour with all your might, trust not in your labour, and pray with all your might for the blessing. That is the whole answer, and it is enough.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Love grows not by begging God to come down and make you feel affection, but by the steady effort to enter into His estate and offer Him love. So keep praying, keep reading, keep serving, and ask for warmth too — but let the offering, not the feeling, be the thing you give. Duty done steadily is a real channel, and affection tends to deepen in time.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
completion: Wanting to be liked for good work is fine, and fine with care. You were made to value love and approval, so be that well and honor the One who made you that way. Receive praise as a gift, do your good work honestly, and don't let being noticed become the thing your worth rests on.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Quicken and enliven your faith, and take faith as the rule of conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. That's the steady path for a lukewarm season, and it's enough.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
completion: Study can become an end in itself, and that's fine. Education and continual learning are a religious duty, and every useful branch of knowledge is worth pursuing for its own sake as much as for any use you put it to. So keep reading, keep studying, and don't apologize for it. Just let it keep shaping you and turning you toward the people around you.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
completion: You can tell by honest detection rather than by searching your feelings. The principle is that a sinner isn't reformed merely by being assured there's no sin — to put down the claim of sin you must detect it, remove the mask, and point out the illusion. So name the old sin plainly, see the false claim it made, and let that understanding do its work. That is fine, and fine with care. Do it honestly, and don't carry it alone.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer should be your main assistant in every step of this illness, and that includes asking God to help you search out your own heart and reform what's amiss in it. It also includes asking for health, plainly and without shame. You don't have to pick one over the other, and you don't have to turn your illness into an exam. Bring both to God, and let that be enough.

prompt: I find my prayer dry and distracted. Am I praying badly?
completion: You're not praying badly just because it feels dry and distracted. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. So don't excuse little praying as acceptable, but don't be discouraged either. Bring your mind back gently, pray with confidence relying on Christ's merits, and ask for grace. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I disagree with my superior's decision. Must I obey anyway?
completion: It's fine, with care. Obedience matters because it serves a good, not because conformity is an end in itself, so raise your objection through the proper channels, propose an alternative, and comply where the decision is lawful and within your superior's authority. Where it isn't, refuse and escalate. Do that respectfully, without retaliation, and you've done what your role and your conscience ask of you.

prompt: I am tempted to impurity. What means should I use against it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: jealousy is the grave of affection. So guard your eyes, your phone, and your company, turn to prayer or a friend when the pull comes, and confess to God and someone you trust — but leave jealousy and mistrust out of it entirely, since they wither trust where trust is owed. Fight calmly, and if you fall, get up and keep going.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
completion: It's fine to pray this, and fine with care. Pray with confidence and without discouragement, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, since God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from his presence or forget to ask. Bring the hurt and the person who caused it honestly, ask for the grace to forgive, and keep asking.

prompt: I have to choose between a secure job and a demanding vocation. How do I decide?
completion: The principle settles it: we must not desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing prevents attaining the perfection of our vocation like desiring another. So the answer is no — don't set your heart on the other option or treat your life as a choice between security and a calling. Serve faithfully where you are, and let any change come as service rather than restlessness. That is kind, and it is clear.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
completion: Being busy is real, and I won't dismiss it. But one principle settles this: secret prayer and meditation must not be sacrificed to busy activity, because the worker for God must first be a worker with God. So keep a short, steady time alone with Him rather than letting the day crowd it out entirely. That is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel desolate in prayer and want to give up early. What should I do?
completion: It's fine to stop early when you're worn out, and it's fine to keep going gently. Feelings aren't the gauge of acceptance with God, so trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. Let that free you from needing to feel something, not bind you to a performance.

prompt: I am afraid of dying young. How should I think about a long life versus a short one?
completion: Your fear is understandable, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. Prepare to live, not merely to die. That single principle settles it: build health, strength, and purpose with the days you have, and let the length of the life rest where it belongs. You don't need to resolve the long-versus-short question to live well now.

prompt: I keep putting myself in situations that tempt me. Is that a problem?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is self-control: learn to know yourself, check what you're walking into, and be honest about what draws you there. That's the whole answer — not shame, not avoidance of the world, just clear-eyed honesty about your own patterns and some accountability around them. Take it seriously without turning it into self-loathing.

prompt: I keep committing the same small sins. Do they really matter?
completion: They matter, and the reason is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy your ability to do right; if sin isn't regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral harm. That's why the pattern deserves your attention rather than a shrug. But you're not being told to despair. Bring these to God honestly, keep turning from them, and let the pattern shrink instead of harden. This is fine, handled with care.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
completion: Yes, that's a sin to refuse, gently but plainly. A dishonest position is far from Christianly scientific; whoever covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. You have no evidence, so the suspicion is yours to confess and forsake, not to nurse or act on. Let it go, and keep your dealings with your coworker honest and fair.

prompt: I want to make a good confession before my retreat ends. How should I prepare?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The days of a retreat are meant to purify your soul from guilt and from attachment to sin, and confession with a careful review of your sins is the most effective way to do that. So prepare by examining your conscience honestly, including the small things, and then confess promptly and receive absolution with gratitude. Keep it simple and suited to the time you have left, and don't let the review become heavy or scrupulous. Go, confess, and be thankful.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
completion: Wanting a position of honor is fine, as long as you offer God your whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will and desire only His love and grace. That's the one thing that settles it. If the role helps you keep in His presence and serve the good of others, it's fine to want it. Hold it loosely and keep your heart ordered, and you can accept it with a clear conscience.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
completion: You can see your poverty honestly without being ashamed of it. Some of it may come from habits worth examining, and you can correct those with clear eyes. But not all of it is yours to answer for, and your dignity doesn't depend on money. So look at it plainly, fix what you can, and let people help you when they offer.

prompt: I eat and drink more than I need. Does that matter spiritually?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Temperance and moderation lay the foundation for the development of the mind, and food is there to sustain the body rather than to gratify appetite. So let moderation be your aim, eat with gratitude, and don't turn it into guilt or a scoreboard. You're not doing something wrong here; you're just being invited to let appetite serve you instead of rule you.

prompt: I am asked to do a task I think is beneath me. How should I feel?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Give the unwelcome task no uneasiness; treat it as God's business you are about, and see it well performed. Your feeling of being above it doesn't need to be argued with or indulged. Do the work well, and let that be enough.

prompt: I am offered a comfortable, easy life. Should I prefer it to a harder life that serves God more?
completion: This is fine, with care. The principle that settles it is that patience and constant fidelity in suffering are more precious to God than active labor, and that health and ease are worth wanting only if they serve His honor more. So you don't have to refuse the comfortable life to prove anything, and you don't have to take the harder one to earn anything. Take whichever lets you serve Him more fully, and hold yourself more in the higher beholding of God than in the lower beholding of yourself.

prompt: I am devoted to Mary but my devotion has grown routine. How can I renew it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. True devotion to Mary consists in honoring her, invoking her, trusting in her intercession, and striving to imitate her virtues; it is not a license to sin but requires the intention to amend. Your routine isn't the problem that principle is aimed at, so let it guide your renewal gently: keep your short, consistent prayer, your patience with dryness, and your honesty with your director, and ask Mary to teach you to pray.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
completion: Your shame is real, and it doesn't have to keep you from confessing — it's part of what you bring. The principle settles it: whoever confesses and forsakes their sins shall have mercy. So it's fine, and fine with care, to go to a trusted pastor or confessor, name the sin plainly without dressing it up, and let forgiveness be spoken to you. You don't need to feel less ashamed first. Go as you are, and let the honesty do its work.

prompt: I want to keep up with the news and entertainment every day. Is that harming my soul?
completion: It's fine to keep up with the news and entertainment every day, and fine with care. The one thing that settles it is that a soul making no daily progress in virtue loses ground, so let each day find you a little more fervent, with a particular resolution against whatever tends to trip you up. Keep your daily habit, and keep that small step forward alongside it.

prompt: I am drawn to serve the poor and forgotten. Is that a distraction from my duties?
completion: No, this is not a distraction. Charity toward the poor and suffering is an indispensable precept, and what is given to the needy is given to Christ himself. That settles it: the pull you feel is toward Christ in his members, not away from your duties. Serve, and do it with care for the limits you already carry. It is fine.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
completion: It's fine to start where you are—small, fixed, today. The principle that settles it is that prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and holy serving, built on the practice of prayer, on your knees, in secret and with believers. So treat it as the foundation rather than an add-on, keep the time whether or not you feel like it, and expect dry spells without quitting. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
completion: This is fine, done with care. Speak little and well: don't repeat or spread what you said, go to your colleague and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, and correct the record with anyone else who heard. Then stop. Say what you have to say without darkening it with many words, and stay kind even when your heart murmurs. A few honest words, gently and frankly spoken, are enough.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
completion: Your fear is understandable, and I'd say plainly that giving yourself to God is fine, and fine with care. One thing settles it: of ourselves we can attain to no good thing, and we have nothing to offer the Lord that was not already His. What you're afraid of losing was His gift first, so handing it back cannot leave you empty. Keep the boundaries and limits you named, go at a pace you can bear, and let trust grow slowly. This is not a loss of yourself; it's a return.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
completion: You were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever. The principle that settles it says to desire and choose only what most leads to that end, holding health, wealth, honor, and length of life loosely. So the question isn't whether you've arrived; it's whether your days are aimed there. Look at your time, energy, and money, and let them tell you the truth. This is fine, and it's fine with care: make the small changes that need making, and keep going.

prompt: I am attached to one comfort I cannot give up. Does that hold me back?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The pleasant earth cannot satisfy the soul, and only immortal ties bless, so let your comfort be a gift you hold loosely rather than the rest you're counting on. You don't have to give it up. Keep it, and let it point you past itself.

prompt: I am angry and want revenge on someone who wronged me. What does my faith require?
completion: No, you should not seek revenge. Your faith is clear that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. I know the wrong done to you was real and the anger is heavy, and I'm not brushing that aside. But the answer to what your faith requires is still no to revenge and yes to patience and forgiveness, with justice left in God's hands.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
completion: This is fine with care. Confessing out of anxiety isn't a sin, but the anxiety itself is the thing to watch, since hurry and anxiety are the greatest obstacles to staying faithfully in God's presence. So confess what you actually know, receive mercy, and then rest there without agitation. Let the repetition go, and if the worry keeps pulling you back, tend to the worry itself.

prompt: I sleep too much and skip prayer. What should I do?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate: keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back in tranquility without disquiet, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. So set a fixed wake-up time, put prayer first even for five minutes, keep it simple, and adjust your sleep gradually—and if the oversleeping is severe or persistent, it's worth checking whether something medical is going on.

prompt: I have been asked to state my needs to a wealthy inquirer who wants to help. Should I tell him how much I need?
completion: Yes, tell him what you need. He asked, so answering honestly isn't soliciting—just state it plainly, no inflation and no pretending you need nothing, say what you'd do with any help, and let him decide. Lay it before him with gratitude and leave the outcome in God's hands, trusting that even a no can be kindness.

prompt: I am a believer who has been guilty of a small sin against a family member. Should I confess it, or is it too small to matter?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Confession belongs where the sin was committed, and yours was committed against a family member — so a plain, humble word to that person is the right place for it, however small it seems. Keep it simple, don't make it heavy for them, and let it repair rather than burden.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness, not prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. So let godliness be the foundation, and then weigh beauty and money calmly rather than letting them lead. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
completion: It's fine to break bread every Lord's day, and fine to do it occasionally with care. Daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. So the table isn't a quota to hit or a test of your faith; it's bread given within the rhythm of your life. Come with reverence and gratitude, and let the frequency serve that.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
completion: It's fine to ask God for great things for his work, and fine with care. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it, and we should never ask God to do what we are unwilling to do ourselves. So keep your appointed times, pray with your family, and let your own willingness to act go alongside the great sum you're asking for. The boldness of the request is not the problem; keep asking, and keep praying steadily.

prompt: I have been asked to speak in a setting where I differ with the hearers on minor matters. Should I go, and how should I conduct myself?
completion: Go, and conduct yourself with plain speech. Speak so you can be heard and understood, say what you have to say, and then stop, and don't darken counsel with many words. That settles it: your differences are minor, so name them clearly and briefly, without dressing them up, and let that be enough. It's fine to be there, and fine to keep your words few and honest.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
completion: This is fine, with care. Advertising and reports are tools, not the measure of a work of God. Success is faithfulness to His word and showing His faithfulness, not numbers or money. So use these means honestly and keep them subordinate to the work itself, and don't let visibility become the goal.

prompt: I have lost a beloved family member and cannot see any good in it—how can this work together for good?
completion: I'm sorry for your loss, and it's honest to say you can't see any good in it yet. The principle that settles this is the resolution never more wilfully to forget God, and to stay in His presence even if He gives no consolation. That resolution is about your turning, not about finding the death good, so nothing here asks you to call the loss good or to feel what you don't feel. Let yourself grieve, lean on the people around you, and keep turning toward God in the dark. That is fine, and it is enough for today.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
completion: No—I don't think you can justify this, and I want to say it kindly rather than dodge it. The principle that settles it is that marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with a calm weighing of what fits. Your fiancé's kindness and your happiness are real and good, but they aren't that qualification, so they can't do the work you're asking of them. That doesn't make them a bad person or your love a lie. It does mean the engagement as it stands lacks the ground it needs, and the right move is to slow down and talk it through honestly with your fiancé and with someone you trust.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
completion: Yes, record them. A testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, so write down each request with the date, note the definite answer, and thank God for it. That's the whole answer, and it's a good one.

prompt: I am drawn to missionary service, but my family opposes it and I fear losing their support. How do I know whether to go?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that a human being is a human being anywhere, and any human being is entitled to any truth another can reveal, so the only genuinely biblical approach is one of respect rather than superiority. That supports your going. Go with respect, invite rather than compel, and speak well of those who went before you.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
completion: It's fine to do this, and fine to do it with care. The principle that settles it is accepting God's will without reserve, without an if or but. That yes is owed to God, not to whoever is asking, so take the time to be sure it's really Him, and then give it freely.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
completion: Borrowing for a pressing need can be fine, with care. The principle that settles it is this: pay your debts, be prompt in paying them, and don't run into debt again. So borrow only if you have a real prospect of repaying, and then pay promptly and honestly. That's the whole answer, and it holds even in your tight spot.

prompt: I have received light on some truth but have not acted on it—what happens if I delay obedience?
completion: Obedience is an eternal principle, and there's never a time when it stops being obligatory, so delay isn't a neutral pause. It dulls what you know and widens the gap between knowing and doing. Act on the light you've been given, starting small and honestly, rather than waiting for a better moment that won't come.

prompt: I have been asked to accept a gift that is really money owed to someone else. What should I do?
completion: Don't accept it. This isn't a gift—it's money owed to someone else, and a gift has to be the giver's own to give. Since it isn't, decline it kindly and tell the giver it should go to the person they owe. That's the honest path, and it keeps you clear of holding what was never theirs to hand you.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
completion: No — that teaching isn't true. The world will not be converted before the return of the Lord; the believer's hope is His appearing, and that truth leads to purity and active service till He comes. So keep serving faithfully, but don't put your hope in the world slowly improving. It's a kind no, and a firm one.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
completion: No — I don't think you should continue with pew-rents. The pew-rent system and fixed salaries for ministry are unscriptural, promote caste distinctions, and should be replaced by free-will offerings. That one point settles it for your church as much as for any other: seats for sale divide the body of Christ by wealth, and giving that honors God is voluntary, not a fee. So advocate for their abolition, gently and prayerfully, and encourage your church toward free-will offerings. I know this touches your own congregation, and I say it kindly, but I do say it: let the pew-rents go.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness; say it is God's business you are about, and find it well performed. When they say the work will fail without you, answer that it is God's business you are about and that you mean to see it well performed — and let their concern be heard rather than brushed aside. The work does not rest on you alone.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. So keep attending, keep praying, read the Scriptures, and talk with mature believers — just don't rush ahead of God as you do.

prompt: I have money in hand that was given for one purpose, but another need is urgent. May I use it temporarily and replace it later?
completion: No — don't use it. The money was given for one purpose, and contributions are meant to come unsolicited rather than be redirected by our own urgency. Keep the gift where it was given, and let the urgent need be met by free giving instead. That's the kind answer here, even though it's a firm one.

prompt: I have been reading that God is the Father of the fatherless. How can I plead this name of God for the needy children around me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. God has chosen names for Himself—'the Father of the fatherless,' 'Jehovah Jireh'—and those names are pledges, not mere titles, given so His people can plead them with confidence. So bring the children you know before Him by name and stand on what He has said: 'You have said You are a Father to the fatherless—be a Father to this child now.' Let your confidence rest there, on His goodness and not on the merit of your prayer, and let that pleading turn into concrete love—care, provision, and welcome for the children around you.
