prompt: I have been asked to preach, but I feel I have nothing of my own to say. Should I use another man's sermon?
completion: Don't use another man's sermon. The greatest sermon is practice, and that settles it: the message you're looking for gets made in you as you pray and work at it, not borrowed from someone else. I know you feel you have nothing of your own to say, and that's a real and honest place to stand. But a short word, fitly spoken, that you actually labored over will serve your people better than a fine sermon that isn't yours. Start small, pray for the Spirit to give you a word in due season, and preach what practice makes in you.

prompt: I am a leader and everyone depends on me—what happens to the work if I am removed?
completion: The Lord's work does not depend on any one man's presence; God can raise up a worthy successor, and no man's presence is indispensable. So your removal does not doom the work, and it is fine to plan for it with care—share what you carry and train those who come after you. You can set the question down without fear.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly afflicted in body, and I wonder whether I should spend more time caring for my health or for my soul.
completion: I'd say no to the part of this that would have you set aside medicine and doctors for your body and trust reading alone to heal you. That counsel I refuse, plainly and kindly, because you are greatly afflicted and your body is not a thing to be abandoned. What I'd keep is your care for your soul, which is real and right. But the choice you're framing isn't one you have to make by giving up your health.

prompt: I have more than I need and wonder whether my spending on myself is excessive—how do I judge my expenses?
completion: It's fine, with care. The question with the Lord isn't how much you have but how you came by it and what you'll do with it, and the more means, the more responsibility. Since you have more than you need, let your giving to the Gospel and the poor keep pace with your spending on yourself, and spend with honest motives. That's the whole answer; your own sense of limit is enough to guide the rest.

prompt: I have been reading that God's word shall not return void. Can I claim this promise for my preaching and witness?
completion: Yes, this is fine with care. Read the promise plainly, because where God's word admits a literal sense you take it, and spiritualizing away a clear promise is like a ship groping into harbor in a snowstorm until it strikes the rocks. Isaiah 55 says God's word will accomplish what He sends it to do, so you can rest your preaching and witness on that and keep preparing, praying, and speaking faithfully, leaving the outcome to Him.

prompt: I have been criticized for the plainness and lack of ornament in the work I oversee. Should I add beauty to it?
completion: Adding beauty is fine, with care. The principle that settles it is this: the poet's art should aim at delicacy of style and conscious excellence, with restrained refinement and subdued reserve. That means any beauty you add should be quiet and deliberate, serving the work rather than answering a critic. Your plainness can stay where it's a strength, and your judgment about what the work is for stays yours.

prompt: I have been a Christian for years, but I feel cold and prayerless at times. Should I stop praying until I feel better?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it; little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe. So your coldness is no reason to stop. Keep praying at your set times, gently and honestly, even when it feels empty.

prompt: I am a minister and wonder whether I should be bound to one place or go wherever doors open—how do I know the Spirit's leading?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The servant of Christ has one Master, and you are guided by the Spirit, not by men, as to time and place of service. That means no rule and no human direction gets to bind you to one place or push you out of it. So pray, test the leading, and hold it loosely. You're free to stay or to go as the Spirit makes it plain.

prompt: I have been asked to join in a work that is not based on scriptural principles. Should I join it or start a new work?
completion: Don't join it. You've said yourself that the work isn't based on scriptural principles, and work and prayer are meant to go together — labour with all your might, pray with all your might, and trust God for the increase. You can't earnestly pray for a blessing on something your conscience already calls wrong. Start the new work instead, slowly and prayerfully, and leave the outcome to God.

prompt: I want to know the secret of a holy and useful life. Where do I begin?
completion: Begin with prayer. That's the one thing that settles it: prayer is the central secret of holy living and holy serving, the corner-stone everything else is built on. So it's fine to start exactly where you are — keep a short, regular time of prayer, alone and with others, and pair it with one small act of service this week. You don't need to wait for anything more.

prompt: I am a leader, and I have been tempted to use funds designated for one part of the work to meet another pressing need. What should I do?
completion: No, don't use those funds for the other need. The money was given for one part of the work, and contributions are to come unsolicited, without a collection that makes money look like the whole point. Bring the pressing need openly to your board and those responsible, and leave it there. That keeps trust whole and honors God.

prompt: I defrauded someone years ago and have since become a believer—must I make restitution, and what if the person is dead?
completion: Make it right. Restitution is the revealed will of God—past wrongs and unpaid vows have to be made good, not just avoided from here on, and the conscience stays uneasy until they are. So restore what you took. If the person has died, give it to their heirs, and if there are none to be found, give it to the Lord through the church or to the poor. Do that, and you'll have done what God actually asked of you.

prompt: I am a parent choosing a school for my child. What should I look for in those who will teach and train my child?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Parents owe their children education in every useful branch, and schools should be established with good teachers who are paid and supported. So look for teachers the school supports and keeps, and for a school that takes the full range of learning seriously. Visit, ask your questions, and trust your judgment about your child's care.

prompt: I have been trusting God for my daily needs, but I am tempted to lay up a store against a time of sickness or old age. Is that wrong?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Trusting God doesn't mean neglecting proper means — honest work and wise saving for sickness or old age are watchfulness, not a lack of faith. The care to take is that your saving doesn't slide into anxious self-reliance; hold it loosely, keep giving, and keep your trust in God rather than in what you've put aside.

prompt: I am a believer, and I have been asked to give an account of my stewardship to those who gave. Is that a burden or a duty?
completion: This is a duty, and a healthy one. You are a steward, not an owner — what you received was entrusted to you for a purpose beyond yourself, so accounting for it to those who gave is part of the trust, not a burden to resent. Prepare honestly, be transparent about mistakes, and don't be defensive. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been blessed with a recovery or an averted calamity—how should I express my thankfulness to God?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Thankfulness for a recovery or an averted calamity is a good thing to express, and the principle that God is gracious and knows our wants settles it: say thank you specifically, in your own words, and let it shape how you live. No formula required.

prompt: I am a servant of God, and I have been tempted to be jealous for my own reputation in the work. How do I become jealous only for God's glory?
completion: This is fine, with care. Jealousy is the grave of affection—mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden—so the thing to watch isn't that you notice your name, but that jealousy over it would quietly kill your love for the people you serve and for God. Name the sting honestly when credit goes elsewhere, turn quickly from the comparing thought, and give others room and confidence. Your zeal for God's honour is worth keeping; just don't let jealousy sit at the wheel.

prompt: I have been reading that God cares for the sparrow. How can I apply this to my own fears about my needs?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Jesus said not one sparrow is forgotten before God and the hairs of your head are numbered—so your fears about your needs are met with a Father who already knows them before you ask. Let that settle the ground under you, and let the habit of praying and thinking of him often do its slow work in you. You don't have to carry the worry alone.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for the removal of an affliction, but I am not sure it is God's will to remove it. How should I submit?
completion: Keep praying for relief, honestly, and keep asking God to show you his will — that's right, and you don't need to be ashamed of wanting healing. But I'd say no, plainly and kindly, to treating your affliction as mainly a mental disturbance while insisting there is no disease. That isn't submission; it's a way of stepping around the very thing you're trying to hand over. Lay your desire before God, add 'not my will but yours be done,' and seek wise counsel about treatment. Let peace guide your next steps.

prompt: I am a young believer, and I want to learn to pray as George Muller did. What are the conditions of prevailing prayer?
completion: This is fine—go ahead and learn from Muller. Prayer is meant to be as simple and constant as a child asking a parent, and God is a Father who delights to be sought for everyday needs, not a God who hides behind man-made rules. So bring him your ordinary requests plainly and often, and let Muller's example point you toward that simple, continual dependence rather than toward a checklist.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
completion: Don't soften it. The work is supported by voluntary contributions sent freely and without asking, because God has supplied all your need and withheld no good thing—so the message never needs to be trimmed to keep the givers content. Preach it whole, and leave the provision to him.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
completion: Start reading, and let the Bible take first place among your books. The Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so read them habitually and prayerfully, and turn what you find into obedience. Set a daily time, pray before you open it, go slowly, and begin somewhere like a Gospel. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been invited to join in Christian work alongside unconverted people—is that acceptable?
completion: This is fine, with care. Christian work is primarily GOD's own work through man, not man's work for GOD, and its highest aspect is obedience to GOD and bringing glory to His Name. Since the work is His and not chiefly yours, joining open, honest labor alongside unconverted people is acceptable—just stay honest about your faith, keep accountability to your church, and decline anything that asks for secrecy or compromise.

prompt: I have been asked to take on a work that will outlive me, and I wonder what will become of it after my death. Should that stop me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection—by keeping that memorial present we learn to die daily. That settles it: you do the work now as someone who knows their time is limited, without demanding control over what comes after. Build in ways for others to carry it forward, and let the outcome go.

prompt: I am a parent and wonder whether my prayers and teaching for my children will bear fruit—should I expect present fruit?
completion: Yes, you may expect present fruit—pray for it and look for it. Children are to be trained in the fear of the Lord with expectation of present fruit, and the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation. So keep praying and teaching, and watch for the small signs now, without measuring yourself by a timetable or a particular form.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
completion: Yes, this loneliness is to be expected, and it doesn't mean you were wrong to follow your conscience. One thing settles it: solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, because the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. So let the ache turn you inward toward that quiet rather than back toward what you left, and be gentle with yourself as you do.

prompt: I am unsure whether to be baptized as a believer—does it affect my standing in the church?
completion: It's fine to be baptized as a believer, and fine to take your time getting there. Baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ; in itself the rite is useless, so it isn't a hoop you must clear to be right with God. Practically, many churches do treat it as the doorway to membership, so talk with your pastor and go forward when you're ready.

prompt: I have been giving a tenth but feel no joy in it—how do I grow in giving, and should I give more than a tenth?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Giving is worship, and God loves a cheerful giver — people give liberally when giving becomes a joy rather than a mere duty. So keep giving your tenth, and give more only as it becomes a joy and as you're able, not out of guilt. The growth you're after is in the heart, and that's the right place to start.

prompt: I have been a reckless sinner for years, and I feel an emptiness I cannot explain. Is there any hope that God could receive someone like me?
completion: Yes, there is hope for you—and the way to it is to acknowledge your wretchedness honestly and return to God with greater trust, not to sit in disquiet. That is the whole answer to your question, and it is a kind one: come back, and come back trusting.

prompt: When I read that God has eyes and hands and walks with the patriarchs, am I to think of him as having a body?
completion: No—don't think of God as having a body. His eyes and hands and walking are human words for what he does, not a description of a shape. Our labour must be with the understanding and not with the senses: a man must cast from himself all phantoms, images, and forms and whatsoever is not God, communing with him by the intelligence and will, not by bodily organs or outward senses. So let the language point you to the living God, not to a picture you carry around. That's the kind answer here, and it's a plain no.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and whether God really knows what I will freely choose.
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the same eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow, either not sending trouble or giving courage to bear it. That meets your anxiety about the future and about God's knowledge of your free choices without demanding you solve it first. Bring your fear honestly, make your choices responsibly, and let this comfort hold you.

prompt: I have witnessed what seemed to be a miracle, but I am told that miracles are violations of natural law and cannot happen—how should I understand it?
completion: What you saw doesn't have to be set against natural law, because a miracle is not a suspension or violation of natural law but an event in nature, extraordinary in itself, wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God. The laws stay in place and God works within them. So you can hold your experience honestly and with care, without forcing a verdict either way.

prompt: Is humility and submission beneath my dignity, or is it something eternal in God himself?
completion: No, humility and submission are not beneath your dignity — this is fine. The first degree of humility is a firm attachment to God so strong that nothing in the world, not even the danger of death, could make you deliberate about committing a mortal sin, and a person held like that is not diminished but made steady. So ask your question honestly and keep your dignity; you are not being asked to think less of yourself, only to be held by something greater.

prompt: I've made promises I'm struggling to keep; can I trust that God keeps his promises even when I fail?
completion: Yes, you can trust that. The guarantee that God will consecrate and preserve you blameless lies in His divine faithfulness—'Faithful is He that calleth you, Who also will do it'—and resting on that gives joy, peace, and confidence. Your struggle with promises is real, but your hope rests on His character, not your track record. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I have never been able to feel God's presence in prayer; can I still claim to know that he exists, or am I only fooling myself?
completion: You're not fooling yourself just because you've never felt God's presence in prayer. Our knowledge of God is real even when it's partial — and that's true of all of it, including yours. Feelings were never the measure. So yes, you can claim to know he exists, and you can do it honestly, with the humility of someone whose knowledge isn't complete. Keep praying as you are, and it may help to talk with a pastor or spiritual director about the dryness.

prompt: I have a friend who says all religions are equally true paths to God; how should I respond without being arrogant?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about the person who has renounced all things having nothing left, from without or from within, to come between God and himself, and yet having to see whether he is a religious in truth or only in name, not clinging to the creature rather than the Creator. That turns the question back on you first, so you can hold your own belief that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life while asking your friend real questions and listening. Disagree without being disagreeable, and keep the relationship ahead of the debate.

prompt: If everything is decreed, why should I bother praying, working, or sharing the gospel?
completion: This is fine — keep praying, working, and sharing. The thing that settles it is that we need only recognize God intimately present with us and address ourselves to Him every moment, begging His assistance for knowing His will in doubtful things and rightly performing those plainly required, offering them before we do them and giving thanks when done. Prayer like that isn't an attempt to overturn a decree; it's conversation with the God who is already near, and that is worth doing regardless of how the question about decrees gets answered.

prompt: I want mercy for my sins, but I also sense I deserve judgment—how can God be both merciful and just?
completion: Your sense of deserving judgment is honest, and mercy is still open to you. The Lord is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed and wounded Him with our sins. So come as you are, turn from the evil, and trust Him—that is fine, and it is the way mercy meets justice at the cross.

prompt: I wonder whether the idea of an absolutely perfect Being really implies that such a Being exists, or whether I am only defining a word.
completion: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: perfection is not attained merely by multiplying exercises of piety and good works; self-love feeds on such practices unless we watch over our hearts, root out habitual imperfections, and give ourselves to God without reserve. Your question about defining a word versus naming a real Being is a fair one, and you're right to keep reason's limits in view. But the principle tells you where perfection actually lives—in watching over your heart and giving yourself without reserve, not in winning a definition. So keep asking, and keep your heart honest while you do.

prompt: I am a student of theology, and I find that the more I study, the less I pray; how do I keep my study from killing my devotion?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is that prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of your time and the heart of your time and strength must be given, with the closet first and study second. So keep your study. You don't need to fear it or abandon it. Just give prayer the first and best of your day, and let your reading follow rather than lead. Do that, and your study won't starve your devotion.

prompt: I want to imitate God, but what does fatherly giving and filial receiving look like in my life?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Receive with a filial and loving heart what our Lord sends from a heart so paternal in its care of your perfection — that's the principle that settles it. Your giving can be generous and your receiving can be honest, and both belong to imitating God as Father in your actual life.

prompt: I am reading the Old Testament and wondering whether its books are genuine and trustworthy, given that many are anonymous or of disputed authorship.
completion: It's fine to keep reading and asking. Our Lord's use of the Old Testament books depends on nothing concerning authorship or date; he appeals to them in their spiritual aspect and testimony to himself, and his references to writers under familiar names involve no fallibility. So let the disputed names rest, and keep your attention on what these books testify to.

prompt: How can God be love if he was alone before creation and had no one to love?
completion: This is fine to ask, and here's the heart of it: love is the attribute by which God is eternally moved to self-communication, rational and voluntary, not mere feeling. That means love didn't start when creation did—there was always a giving and receiving within God's own life, so He was never without someone to love. Your instinct that love needs a beloved is right; it just doesn't require a creature to supply it. Ask it freely, and hold it gently.

prompt: I feel I must choose between trusting my own reason and trusting the church; is there another authority?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Authority means weight, what carries weight with your judgment, and the church's authority is not greater for adding coercive power, for believing under threat of pain is not believing on the church's authority at all. So you don't have to choose between your reason and the church; weigh both honestly, and let what is true and loving carry the weight it deserves.

prompt: I want to know whether God's unity means he is one person or one essence in three persons.
completion: This is fine to ask, and the answer is one essence in three persons. Scripture recognizes three as God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and describes them as distinct persons, so God's unity can't mean a single solitary person. That settles it: one divine essence, three persons.

prompt: I want to ask God for things, but does his power mean he must do everything he can, or can he choose to limit himself?
completion: Yes — he can choose to limit himself, and that is good news for your praying. All power belongs to God; it is his, not a force that has to fire whenever it could. So you are not pulling a lever when you ask. Ask boldly, ask specifically, and trust a free and good Father with the how and the when. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I want to know whether the atonement was necessary on God's account or only on mine.
completion: This is fine to ask, and the answer is that the Atonement belongs to the whole of Christian truth: sin as alienation and guilt, sacrifice as expiation and reunion, and Christ as our representative Priest and victim. That one principle settles it—the need is real on both sides of a broken relationship, and Christ meets it as both priest and victim. So you don't have to choose between God's account and yours. Ask it freely.

prompt: If Jesus claimed to be one with God, was he not either a deceiver or deluded rather than divine?
completion: This is fine to ask, and fine to pursue with care. One principle settles it: Christ's testimony to himself cannot be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God and the revealer of God to men. The two-option framing simply doesn't hold, so weigh the evidence honestly and let it lead where it leads.

prompt: I want to be honest, but I wonder whether truth is just whatever God decides to command—does that make truth arbitrary?
completion: No—truth isn't arbitrary, and the reason is simple: truth in God is that attribute by which his being and his knowledge eternally conform to each other, and truth of being precedes truth of knowing. His commands express what he eternally is, so they can't be a random decree. That's why your honesty still matters and still has somewhere solid to stand. You can trust that.

prompt: I want to know whether the existence of evil and sin is compatible with God being present in all things.
completion: This is fine to ask, and fine to hold with care. God does not cause a man to sin, be sick, or die, and it is contrary to our highest ideas of God to suppose He arranges evil results and then punishes the helpless. That one point settles it: His presence in all things is not the presence of an author of evil, so the two are compatible even though the full picture stays beyond you. Keep the question, and keep your trust in His goodness.

prompt: Skeptics say Christianity spread by natural social causes; how do I weigh that against the obstacles of persecution and the offence of the cross?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Doubt is a nearly inevitable stage in the development of thoughtful Christians, so meet the skeptics' case with sympathy and an orderly look at the history rather than a quick dismissal. Lay the natural causes alongside the obstacles honestly, and let the persecution and the offence of the cross stand as real barriers that social factors alone don't fully explain. You can hold both without forcing a verdict on yourself.

prompt: I am a new Christian, and I feel overwhelmed by all the doctrines; do I need to understand them all to grow?
completion: No, you don't need to understand every doctrine to grow. The principle that settles it is that theology must take a new development, standing firm in old truths while the Church assimilates new knowledge rather than multiplying dogmas. That's the Church's long work, not a burden for someone new to the faith. Start with the essentials, who God is, who Jesus is, what he did, and how to follow him, and grow through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship. Let the rest come in time.

prompt: I have an idea of infinity, but is my idea itself infinite, or only finite—and does that matter for proving God?
completion: Your idea is finite, and that's fine. God's infinity means he has no limits or bounds, not merely no known limits—so your concept was never going to be the thing it points to, and it doesn't need to be. A finite mind reaching toward the unlimited is exactly what you described, and it's enough. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I want to know whether the death of Christ on the cross has anything to do with understanding the universe as a whole.
completion: This is fine, with care. The cross shows the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues, and that is a moral claim about God's character, not a map of the physical universe. So let it shape how you understand what the whole is for, and let it stay there. Rest your hope on Christ Himself rather than on your own frames and feelings, and you'll be on steady ground.

prompt: I have been reading about evolution, and it seems to leave no room for a Creator; how should I think about God's work in nature?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The evolutionary origin of man is no threat to theology, since the Creator is immanent in every phase of matter and the method of His working is of no controversial importance. So you can keep reading evolution honestly and keep asking about God without forcing the two into a fight, and let your questions about purpose stay open as you go.

prompt: I am overwhelmed by my sin—can a finite Savior ever be enough to save me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. If your confidence is languishing on account of the number and magnitude of your sins, remember that all is possible to God, that it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one, and that of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. You are not too much for Him to forgive.

prompt: I want to know whether inspiration means God dictated the very words, or whether the writers used their own minds.
completion: Inspiration is the Spirit's influence on the minds of the Scripture writers, making their writings a trustworthy record of progressive revelation sufficient to lead the honest inquirer to Christ and salvation. That settles it for your question: the writers used their own minds, and the Spirit's work on those minds is what makes what they wrote trustworthy. So it's fine to hold both—no need to choose between dictation and human thought. You can rest easy here.

prompt: I want to know whether the resurrection of Christ really happened in the body, or whether the disciples only saw his spirit or had a vision.
completion: This is fine to ask, and fine to explore with care. One principle settles it: the resurrection, his coming forth from the sepulchre in body as well as in spirit, is demonstrated by evidence as varied and conclusive as what proves any single fact of ancient history, and without it Christianity itself is inexplicable. So the bodily claim is not something to set aside as if the spirit were enough. You can bring your honest doubt to it and still take the evidence seriously.

prompt: I am tempted to think that the God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; how do I reconcile them?
completion: It's fine to hold both, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the Old Testament is on a lower level than the New. God condescends to a low stage of conscience and worship, tolerating what was not His original will, and the Old Covenant is gradual and progressive while the New is final. So the difference you feel is real, but it's the difference between preparation and completion, not between two Gods. Read the Old as pointing forward to Christ, and let the tension stay honest rather than forced.

prompt: Should I stop agonizing over whether I am elect and just use the means of grace?
completion: Yes—stop agonizing and use the means of grace. The appointed means must continue to be used even when no immediate benefit can be discerned; formalism is going through the motions without any desire for spiritual profit, not the plain act of praying and reading and worshiping when it feels dry. So bring your unsettled question along with you into those practices, and leave the secret of election to God.

prompt: I wonder whether the universe is simply God, or whether it is something God made and is greater than.
completion: This is fine to ask, and here is the short of it. God is All-in-all, and the only realities are the divine Mind and idea. So the universe is not a second thing God made and then stood outside of, and it is not simply God either. It is an expression of the divine Life, real because God is real, and never greater than its source. You can hold that without fear.

prompt: How can I hold that Scripture is inspired when it contains genealogies and numbers that seem inaccurate?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The unity of Scripture across so many authors and centuries is inexplicable without a superhuman intelligence behind it, so the Bible's inspiration doesn't hinge on every genealogy or number reading like a modern record. Hold to inspiration, study honestly, and let the difficult passages be difficult without losing your footing.

prompt: I was raised to believe in God, and the arguments seem only to confirm what I already held; is that a legitimate way to believe?
completion: Yes, this is a legitimate way to believe, and it's fine with care. Belief in God is not the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are the modes in which faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not the means of creating faith. Being raised in belief and finding the arguments confirm it is exactly that pattern, so you don't need to apologize for it. Keep testing and asking honest questions, and let the confirmation be a strength rather than a substitute for thought.

prompt: Does God's decree mean I had no choice when I sinned?
completion: No — God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you stay responsible. But the decree doesn't lock you in either. God commands all people everywhere to repent now, and since he commands it, the power to renounce sin is available this moment. The feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. So don't wait to feel more or grieve more before you turn, and don't treat the decree as an excuse. Confess it, turn from it now, and trust that the God who commands your holiness supplies what he commands.

prompt: I'm drawn to pantheism because it makes God close, but I fear losing his personal holiness.
completion: Your fear is telling you the truth. Idealistic pantheism errs in denying God's personality and transcendence, and its idea of God is self-contradictory; it gives no sufficient cause for personal intelligences and it contradicts our moral and religious natures by denying freedom, responsibility, prayer and hope of immortality. So the answer is no. Don't trade the living, holy God for a closeness that leaves no one to pray to. Keep the nearness you long for, and keep the God who is distinct from all he made.

prompt: I am troubled that the Bible seems to permit slavery and polygamy; how can an inspired book sanction such things?
completion: I hear the worry, and it's a fair one. The Bible records and regulates slavery and polygamy rather than pretending they don't exist, and regulation is not endorsement. What settles it for me is that love in the New Testament is the outgoing of the entire nature in self-sacrificing service, more than sentiment or desire, and the supreme proof of the reality of our Christian profession. Held against that, those practices stand exposed as less than God's best, and Scripture's whole direction moves past them. So keep asking your question with care; it's a good one, and it won't undo your faith.

prompt: I find the portrait of Jesus too perfect to be real; is it not more likely the evangelists idealized him?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to keep reading with care. The Christ-ideal viewed only as a human masterpiece would be the despair of mankind, like the genius of Kant which mocks imitation; it is as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life is the hope of all the ages. That's the thing to weigh as you read: a merely polished ideal would be beautiful and useless, so the perfection you notice is a claim, not just a flaw in the sources. Hold your question honestly, and let the portrait answer for itself.

prompt: I want to know whether the Spirit is a person I can grieve and resist, or just an influence.
completion: Yes, the Spirit is a person you can grieve and resist, not a mere influence. One thing settles it: your own spirit loves truth and virtue but gets overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. That means the grieving and resisting are personal and close to home, happening in the middle of your own struggle. So take him as a person, and take your own heart seriously, because the one you resist is the one trying to enlighten you.

prompt: I want to know whether the apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies undermines the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation.
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prophecy is foretelling by direct communication from God, and its proof lies under your eyes and grows with each new fulfilment, which means an apparent failure is a real question you may press rather than something to brush aside. Keep the limits you set, weigh context and genre honestly, and let neither a single miss nor a single hit carry the whole case.

prompt: I feel that Confucius and Buddha offer noble teaching; why should I regard their systems as defective?
completion: You're right that there's real nobility there, and I wouldn't take that from you. But the principle that settles it is this: heathen moral systems are defective because they furnish no sufficient example, rule, motive, or end, and do not recognize man's depravity or dependence on divine grace. That is a claim about defect, not about worthlessness, so your admiration and the defect can both stand. This is fine, and fine with care: honor what is noble, and be clear that it is not sufficient.

prompt: I fear that if God's will made right and wrong, he could have made cruelty good—can that be?
completion: Your fear is worth taking seriously, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. The principle that settles it: do not fear God as though he wished to harm you, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do you great good. That doesn't pretend your question is silly—it just moves you from a maybe about cruelty to the character of the one you're trusting. Keep asking, but don't let the hypothetical turn into fear of a God who means you harm.

prompt: I want to be a good person, but I'm not sure why—is it because it makes me happy, because it's useful, or because God is holy?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The joy of God's personal love isn't earned by merit, good works, or charitable effort—it comes through a grateful, longing attitude toward God that you keep up. So let happiness and usefulness be companions on the road, not the reason you walk it. Root yourself in God's holiness, stay warm toward the people in front of you, and keep going gently when goodness costs you something.

prompt: I want to know whether my love for others should be guided by what they want or by what they truly need.
completion: This is fine, with care. Love is discerning, not blind — it abounds in full knowledge and all discernment so it can tell good from bad, better from best. That's the principle that settles it: you don't follow wants blindly and you don't impose needs blindly. You weigh both with the person, and you keep their say over their own life intact. Offer what you think they need as an invitation, not a decree.

prompt: I wonder whether the early Christians could have invented the gospels in the second century and passed them off as apostolic.
completion: It's fine to ask, and the answer is that a second-century invention is very hard to square with what the gospels actually contain. The gospel cannot be a mythical outgrowth of Jewish ideas, because in its main features it runs directly counter to Jewish expectations: a gospel for all nations and a suffering Messiah were contrary to the sullen nationalism and temporal hopes of the Jews. That one point settles it, and it leaves your question where it belongs—open to honest historical inquiry, which is exactly where you're standing.

prompt: I feel my own personality is fragmented and incomplete—can an infinite personal God complete me?
completion: Yes, this is fine. Personality means the power of self-consciousness and self-determination, and God is self-conscious and self-determining in the highest degree — so the completion you're asking about doesn't erase you, it makes you more truly yourself. Your sense of fragmentation is real, and it doesn't disqualify the question; it's exactly the ground the question grows from. Go gently, at a pace you can bear, and let that be enough.

prompt: I am a materialist and think mind is produced by the brain—how do I answer the claim that mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter?
completion: I'd say no to this one, gently but without hedging. The argument you're being offered rests on the principle that either Mind produces or it is produced, and that like produces like, so mind cannot come from matter. But that principle only bites if mind is first, and you've told me you don't think that. Taking it up would mean setting aside your materialism to win the exchange, which isn't a defense at all. Keep the honest part: thinking does feel different in kind from matter, and that's worth saying. Just don't let the feeling be promoted into proof. Ask why the feeling should track reality rather than being the brain's own account of itself, and leave it there.

prompt: I'm told to love my neighbor, but why should I be moral at all—what makes right actually binding on me?
completion: This is fine to ask, and the answer holds: the ground of moral obligation is the holiness of God, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things—we are bound to the right because God is it, not merely because he wills it. That's what makes right binding on you, and it's why loving your neighbor isn't arbitrary. You can keep asking the question; the answer is that the good you're bound to is a Person, not a rule.

prompt: Has Christianity actually done good in the world, or is that just what believers claim for their own religion?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it hard. The evidence Christianity offers isn't a boast — it's the power of sins forgiven and lives actually regenerated, which you can look at in real people rather than take on trust. So weigh it that way, by lives and not by slogans, and let the honest question stand.

prompt: How could a religion preached by unlearned men, centered on a crucified Jew, conquer the Roman Empire unless God was in it?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to see providence in the spread of the faith. One thing settles how to frame it: the victory of the party that recognized the whole Old Testament as the revelation of the Christian God was not due to Jewish Christian influence, and Jewish Christianity's existence would only have made that victory harder had it not already fallen into the background. So keep your wonder at the transformation of the empire, and let go of the assumption that the first Jewish believers simply handed the scriptures on and settled the matter. Ask your question; just let the history be what it was.

prompt: Why were whole nations and cities destroyed by God in ancient times?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to answer it with care. God's hand is over all, and he will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though he did not foreordain the wickedness that brought them; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. That one principle settles it: the destruction came from human evil, and God's foreknowledge is not the same as his authorship. So hold both truths, the gravity of what happened and the goodness of God's purpose, and don't shrink either one.

prompt: Why did God give me a body, and does it matter what I do with it?
completion: It's fine, and it's fine with care. The body is for the Lord and the Lord for the body, so your body isn't a random container but the place where a real union with the risen Christ happens. That's why what you do with it matters, and why you can approach it with care rather than fear.

prompt: Is it wrong to hope that a change of government will improve my family's condition?
completion: Hoping your family's condition improves is fine, and it's fine with care. A change in the form of government does not materially better the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, not the products of republics or monarchies. So hope, and work for better days, but don't rest your family's future on who holds office, and keep tending your own people and planning for them as you go.

prompt: If human governments have failed for so long, why should I trust any new political movement to fix things?
completion: No — don't trust a new political movement to fix things, and I mean that kindly. Human schemes to regenerate the world, changes of government among them, are incompetent because like causes produce like effects and the materials will not combine. A fresh movement is the same material under a new name. So keep your skepticism, judge proposals and leaders on their merits, and do the nearer work of governing yourself well.

prompt: Where is heaven, and where will the saints reign with Christ?
completion: This is fine. One principle settles it: the earth is man's eternal inheritance, the saints will reign on the earth, and the New Jerusalem will descend to a purified earth where God dwells with men. So heaven isn't a distant escape, and the reign with Christ belongs to a renewed earth. Hold that with care, and it's fine.

prompt: I want to help the poor and reform society—what means are actually adequate to the task?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that poverty comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means—so your means should include teaching prudence and thrift alongside food, shelter, and fair laws. Keep the care: the destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and people are esteemed by character, not wealth. That's the whole answer, and it's a yes.

prompt: Is this earth my final home, or am I destined for some far-off heaven?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine to hold it as hope rather than certainty. God willeth that we be occupied in knowing and loving till we be fulfilled in Heaven, and the nearer we be to our bliss the more we long after it. Your longing isn't a fault to be cured; it's a sign of where you're headed. So you can keep asking the question and keep hoping, without needing to force an answer today.

prompt: What is the purpose of my existence on this earth?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. You were made to praise, reverence, and serve God, and everything else on earth exists to help you toward that end, so the question you're asking is the right one to ask. Let that end order your choices, and let your longing for a lasting home be what it is: nature's own voice in you, not a flaw. Take your time with it, and be gentle with yourself while you do.

prompt: Did my spirit exist before I was born, and will it live after death?
completion: This is fine to ask, and the answer is yes on both counts. You are an eternal being, body and spirit, existing before birth and after death, and both are needed to be a perfect man. So your spirit did not begin at birth and will not end at death. Hold that with care, and let it steady you rather than make you anxious.

prompt: Am I responsible for the sins of my fathers, or for the sins of my nation?
completion: You're not personally guilty for sins you never committed—Ezekiel 18 is clear that each person answers for his own—but you are responsible for how you respond to what your family and nation handed down. Christ gave Himself for your sins, purchasing them and you, so your sins belong to Him and not to you, and you are accepted in the Beloved. That settles the ground you stand on, so you can face the inheritance honestly: confess it, resist it, don't repeat it, and act faithfully where you have influence. This is fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: Why do revolutions and republics not make people happier?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it with care. A change in the form of government does not materially better the people's condition, because happiness and peace are gifts of God, not products of republics or monarchies. That is the whole answer to why revolutions and republics leave people no happier, and it is reason enough to stop expecting them to.

prompt: Is there hope for my ancestors who died in ignorance or idolatry?
completion: Yes, there is hope, and you can hold it without pretending. Just don't look to death to work a miracle, as though simply dying opens paradise; in character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. So commend your ancestors to God's mercy, pray for them, and grieve not as those without hope, because Christ has touched the bier and spoken peace. That is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Is it unjust for God to punish me for circumstances I could not control?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it honestly. Misfortune, illness, and strife are not to be charged to God's will — they come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, though God permits them and turns them toward good. So no, God is not punishing you for what you couldn't control. Bring the question, and let the blame come off both God and you.

prompt: Should I obey and pray for rulers I did not choose and who may be wicked?
completion: Pray for them. Intercession for rulers and all in authority is a foremost duty, exactly because the peace of the world and the quiet life of ordinary people rest on leaders whose burdens outrun human wisdom and who need God's guidance. Praying for someone you didn't choose and may not trust is not endorsement — it's asking God to give them wisdom and restrain injustice. So pray sincerely, obey in lawful things for conscience' sake, and refuse only what is truly wicked. That holds whether the ruler is good or bad, and it's fine.

prompt: Is it right to rebel against an unjust government to establish righteousness?
completion: It can be right, but only in extreme cases. Christian citizens owe obedience to civil authority for conscience' sake, yet resistance to unlawful power may in extreme cases be a right. So if a government truly tramples basic rights and leaves no peaceful recourse, resisting it can be justified, but only with great care and after everything else has been tried.

prompt: Why do the sects of Christendom disagree so bitterly among themselves?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it carefully. The principle that settles it is that all who contend fiercely about the kingdom of Christ and slander and persecute one another for religion have not yet known Christ. That means the bitterness is the real problem, not the question. So look at the divisions honestly, keep your own convictions, and refuse the contempt. You don't need to pretend the differences don't matter, and you don't need to surrender what you think is true. Ask your question, and ask it with humility.

prompt: Why does religion often seem so melancholy and forbidding?
completion: It's fine to notice that religion often feels melancholy and forbidding, and fine to say it. The reason is that people keep it indoors as their own feelings about themselves, and the remedy is the open air of the soul: God's mercy is objective to us, as free as the sunshine and as near as the open air, not something we manufacture by brooding. Your observation stands, and so does the way out of it.

prompt: Why is the earth cursed, and will the curse ever be lifted?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and here's the heart of it: it would be unreasonable, unjust, unscriptural, and would frustrate God's designs for the world to remain forever under the curse and under Satan's usurped dominion. So the curse is real, but it isn't forever. Hold that with care, and don't try to schedule or engineer its lifting yourself.

prompt: Why does God permit evil and suffering if he is all-powerful?
completion: Asking this is fine, and fine to hold without a neat answer. The one thing that settles it for me is that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end — it could not be at all except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. That doesn't make the pain good or answer every why, and it isn't meant to. It means you can bring the question honestly and still commit what you can't understand to His providence.

prompt: Is God a distant and gloomy being, or can I approach him as a father?
completion: You can approach him as a father. God is the Father of our spirits and you stand to him as a child; his service is not gloomy but cheerful, and he is near to those who ask him. That settles it, and it's fine, with the care a child still owes a father.

prompt: Was Christ's kingdom set up at his first coming, or is it still future?
completion: No, I would not answer it the way you've framed it, and I want to be kind about why. The kingdom of God is revealed from heaven and established by God himself, not built by human means, and that principle is true. But it doesn't hand you a clean either/or, and I won't pretend it does. So the honest answer is: don't press this into a simple verdict. Hold the hope, and leave the timing with God.

prompt: Why is there to be a gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and a separate gathering of the saints to Zion?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Unity and cooperation are the strength of Zion, but unity does not mean individual uniformity; the Saints should be of one heart and one mind while each fills his own calling. That settles it: the gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion are two purposes with two places, and the difference between them is not a rivalry or a ranking. Hold both in view, and let each person fill his own calling without turning the distinction into a division.

prompt: Was Queen Victoria lawfully anointed of God, or is her authority merely human?
completion: No, Victoria was not lawfully anointed of God, and we should not say she was. No ruler now is legally called and anointed of God; the anointing by unauthorized ministers is a farce, and the authority is merely human. God may overrule a ruler, but that is not the same as anointing one. So the honest answer is a plain no: her authority is human, not divine, and it is wrong to dress it up as God's own commissioning.

prompt: Why did Jesus say his kingdom is not of this world if it is to be on the earth?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is that Jesus was describing where his kingdom comes from, not where it will end up. The kingdom of God will be a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth, not a mere spiritual or inward reign, with laws, officers, and resurrected saints. So 'not of this world' points to its heavenly source and authority, while its future is still a visible reign on the earth. That settles it.

prompt: Will there be a reckoning for the way rulers and priests have abused their authority?
completion: Yes, and the reckoning is built into the thing itself. The priesthood cannot be exercised in any degree of unrighteousness, and its power will not abide with the corrupt or the treacherous. So the authority abusers lean on is already slipping from them, and God humbles the proud and lifts the oppressed. That is a real answer to your question, and it is a kind one.

prompt: How will the kingdom of God be established—by human effort or by revelation from heaven?
completion: It's fine to ask, and the answer holds both truths together. The kingdom is revealed from heaven—God himself establishes it through a restored gospel, a standard lifted to the nations, a literal Zion, and judgements on the wicked, not by human means. Within that, it develops gradually and calls for individual labor, the central business of the Saints. Revelation starts it; your labor serves it. That's the whole answer, and it's a good one to live by.

prompt: Why are people in rich countries still unhappy and violent?
completion: It's fine to ask why rich countries are still unhappy and violent, and fine to answer with care. The principle that settles it is that the poor are the people of God and have as good a right to your food as anyone—so the answer has to name who is being honored and who is being left outside, not just stress and consumerism. That's the whole of it: ask honestly, answer with the dignity of the least in view, and don't shrug.

prompt: Who has the right to govern the earth, and do any present kings have that right?
completion: God alone has the right to govern the earth, and no present king holds that right — none was legally called and anointed of God, and the anointing they claim is a farce. That's the whole answer to what you asked, and it's meant kindly: don't go looking for a throne with heaven's seal on it, because there isn't one.

prompt: Is socialism or a community of goods the answer to the misery I see around me?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care, to want a community where everyone is industrious, faithful, and prudent, living within their means. That's a good thing to build toward, and it doesn't ask you to stop caring about the people you see hurting.

prompt: Why does the world seem so full of confusion and misery when God's works are so orderly?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and I'd say it gently: the confusion you see is often the reflection of a heart trying to hold God with the soul and the world with the heart at the same time. The answer isn't rags in a desert. It's learning, right where you are, to put God first with an inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. That is enough to settle where to look, and it's a fine thing to ask.

prompt: What is the meaning of the stone cut out of the mountain without hands?
completion: The stone cut out without hands means God's kingdom, divine in origin and not the product of human power—and it's fine to take that further, as a soul yielded to the Carver in prayer, asking Him to form His image in you. That reading is fine, and fine with care: keep the kingdom meaning at the center, and let the personal picture serve it rather than replace it.

prompt: Why do the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper?
completion: This question is allowed, and it's fine to ask it with care. One thing settles it: virtues born in prosperity are of little value, while those born amid afflictions are strong and firm, and God often gives His servants only the honor of suffering much and carrying the cross. So the righteous aren't abandoned in their pain, and the wicked aren't blessed in their ease. Ask honestly, and hold the people who are hurting gently.

prompt: What will the reign of God on earth actually change for ordinary people?
completion: Yes, it's fine to expect real change for ordinary people. This earth is man's eternal inheritance; the Saints will reign on the earth, and the New Jerusalem will descend to a purified earth where God will dwell with men. So the change is tangible, not just inward, and you can hold that hope with care.

prompt: Why should I wait patiently for the Lord instead of trying to force change myself?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Waiting on the Lord doesn't mean doing nothing; it means being slow to force a step and quick to bring each one to Him in prayer. The true workman waits for the Master's signal before moving, and that's the posture your question already shows. Keep your heart soft and your hands open, and let patience do its work rather than anxiety.

prompt: What am I, and what happens to me when I die?
completion: This is fine to ask, and here is the answer that settles it: death is the door to a higher state, your identity is preserved, and the body will be raised again. So you are not facing an ending, and you need not mourn as those without hope. Ask it plainly and take heart.

prompt: Why is it robbery to take from the rich and give to the poor by force?
completion: No — taking from the rich by force to give to the poor is wrong. Wealth is generally the fruit of labor, industry, and talent, and to seize it by force or legislation is robbery; it would crush the enterprise that produces anything to give. Help the poor freely and generously, but never by force.

prompt: Will Satan always rule over the world, or will he be bound?
completion: No, Satan will not always rule. He is a usurper under God's control, permitted for a season to develop man's weakness and the effects of evil, but he will be bound and cast out. That is the plain answer to what you asked, and it is a kind answer: his rule is temporary, and God's kingdom will prevail.

prompt: How can I know the doctrine is of God rather than of men?
completion: Your question is a good one, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. Men are established in the truth not by signs, miracles, and visions but by humility and faithful obedience to the commandments and laws of God, receiving the testimony line upon line through the still small voice of the Spirit. So keep testing honestly, keep obeying what you already know, and let the quiet witness grow in you over time rather than waiting for something dramatic to settle it.

prompt: What happens to those who died without ever hearing the gospel?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to hope along these lines, with care. The gospel is to be preached to the dead: those who died without hearing it will hear it in the spirit, and work for the dead is carried on in temples. That's the comfort here, and it's a real one. Hold it as hope rather than certainty, since Scripture doesn't give us a detailed map, and keep sharing the gospel with the living.

prompt: Will the earth be restored to its former glory, and what will that look like?
completion: Yes, it will be restored. The restoration of all things means the earth comes back to its primeval glory—one land, fruitful, without curse—and man restored with it. That's what it will look like: creation healed, people whole, the curse gone. Hold that hope; the timing and the details belong to God.

prompt: Why do Christian nations go to war with one another and pray to the same God for victory?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to sit with it. War and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and peace comes only through the gospel. That one truth settles it: the tragedy of two nations praying to the same God for victory is a human tragedy, not a sign that faith is empty. Let the question move you toward peacemaking, and let it be asked honestly.

prompt: Will I see my family and children again in the world to come?
completion: This is a fine hope, and you can hold it with care. The world to come is the restoration of creation, not its erasure, and families and children belong within that restored order. Grieve honestly and hope steadily, and leave the timing and the details with the Father who restores all things.

prompt: How should I live now in light of the coming kingdom of God?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One thing settles it: unless you become like a little child, hanging on Christ for all things, you cannot enter the kingdom, and that is the shortest way. So live that way, dependent and honest about your limits, and let your prayer, generosity, and mending of relationships grow out of that trust rather than out of striving to earn your place.

prompt: Will God punish the world in the last days, and will he warn us first?
completion: Yes. God warns before he punishes, as he did through Enoch, Noah, Lot, and the prophets, and it would be unjust to punish the ignorant without warning. So the warning comes first, and the judgment it warns about is real.

prompt: Can I find peace and happiness by moving to a new country with plenty of food and land?
completion: Wanting peace and happiness is a good instinct, so don't be ashamed of it. But this world is a Touchstone and Finding-place for God, and whoever obeys the law of finding God from this world, rather than waiting to try from the next, alone grasps true Happiness. A new country with food and land can ease real burdens, and that's fine. Just don't expect the move itself to give you peace, because peace is a gift you receive and practice, not something a place produces. Go with care, and keep seeking where you land.

prompt: Why is chastity so important, and what are the eternal consequences of impurity?
completion: Chastity is a most precious treasure, and that one truth settles it. A treasure is protected by prayer, by mortification, by modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by avoiding the occasions of temptation, since he who loves danger shall perish in it. So yes, ask your question, and hear the answer kindly: impurity wounds the soul's union with God, and unrepented it ends in eternal loss, while purity of heart opens the way to the vision of God. Guard the treasure.

prompt: What is Zion, and should I gather to it?
completion: Zion is a people and a place of holiness, and the cause of Zion should be uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love, with other interests taking their proper place. That's the principle that settles it. Gathering can be worthwhile, and it's fine with care—keep your family, work, and finances in view, and don't let any group demand unhealthy sacrifice or isolation. The choice is yours, and you can live a good life either way.

prompt: What is the point of peace societies and congresses if war keeps breaking out anyway?
completion: It's fine to keep supporting peace societies and congresses, and here's the one thing that settles it: war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design. If war were built into the way things are meant to be, these efforts would be pointless. Since it isn't, work that keeps peace before people and builds habits of negotiation is aiming at something real — it just can't promise that war will never break out again. So hold them up with clear eyes about what they can and can't do.

prompt: Can the spread of Christianity as it is now preached bring about a millennium of peace?
completion: No, it can't — not as it's now preached. The peace the angels announced was never a facile worldly peace; it is for those who submit to Christ as Saviour and King, repent, and live by His laws, and nominal Christianity has failed, not Christianity itself. So the honest answer to your question is a gentle but clear no: don't expect the spread of the message as it stands to bring a millennium of peace.

prompt: I've been faithful in doing good for years but I don't feel any special insight. Does obedience really lead to understanding?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Obedience is how you keep in touch with God—that's the principle that settles it—and it never promised that insight would arrive on your schedule. Keep doing good, keep the relationship, and let understanding come as it comes.

prompt: What does it mean that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath?
completion: It means the Sabbath was given to serve people's good, not to crush them — and that is fine, fine with care. The day is to be kept holy and not robbed, with its worship and its duties attended to, so 'made for man' is not permission to set the day aside. It is a word about the day's purpose, and it holds.

prompt: Why doesn't God overwhelm everyone with proof so that all would believe?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is that belief in God is not the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem — religion existed before argument, and the proofs are how faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not the means of creating faith. That's why God doesn't overwhelm everyone with proof: it wouldn't produce the trust he's after. So your question is welcome, and the answer is that overwhelming proof was never the thing that would do it.

prompt: My church seems to care more about its building and budget than about people. How should I respond?
completion: This is fine to raise, and fine with care. Church revenues and treasures exist for the relief of the poor, so asking whether your congregation's resources actually reach people in need is a faithful question, not a disloyal one. Bring it calmly and specifically to your leaders, and offer to help.

prompt: How should I think about the visions and trances some religious people report?
completion: This is fine with care. Visions and trances are reported across many traditions, and the question is how to hold them. The principle that settles it: false mysticism errs by seeking direct communication from God apart from the external means of nature and Scripture, and by passively absorbing human activity into the divine. So take the reports seriously without treating them as automatically authoritative, test any message against Scripture and the counsel of a mature community, and keep your reason and will awake. Look at the fruits—humility, love, obedience—and be wary of claims that demand followership or money. If distress is involved, a pastor or spiritual director, and a mental health professional, can help.

prompt: The prophets seem obsessed with social injustice. Is that really central to Scripture?
completion: Yes, social injustice is central to Scripture. The prophets speak for God when they condemn those who oppress the poor and force their labor to serve another's pomp and vanity, and they say such things are done to Christ himself and fall under his severe judgment. Tested by the Scriptures as the only standard, this is no side issue. It's fine to hold that justice is central, and fine to hold it with care alongside the rest of what Scripture teaches.

prompt: Are there things God won't reveal to us yet because we aren't morally ready for them?
completion: It's fine to wonder about this, and fine to hold it gently. We should leave the beholding of what the secret Deed shall be and not busy ourselves to know God's privy counsels, for the more we busy us the farther we are from knowing. So trust the hidden to God's goodness, grow in honesty about your own limits, and give yourself to what's already been made plain to you.

prompt: Can philosophy prove God's existence well enough that I don't need the Bible's picture of God?
completion: No, philosophy can't prove God's existence well enough to replace the Bible's picture of God, and you shouldn't expect it to. The argument from a perfect Being only gives you an ideal conclusion: it tells you what God would have to be if God exists, not that God does exist. That's the limit, and it's a real one. Philosophy can still clear away objections and show that faith isn't unreasonable, but it can't give you the God you're asking about. For that you still need revelation.

prompt: If God is all-powerful, why does he seem so limited in the Old Testament?
completion: Nothing is too great for God's power and nothing too small for his love. That one truth settles it. The God who cares about trifles is not limited by the vivid, human-shaped language of the Old Testament; he is meeting people where they were, and he is not too grand to care about the small things in your life either. So your question is fine to ask, and fine to keep asking—kindly, and without fear.

prompt: Jesus said he had many things to say that his disciples couldn't bear yet. Does God still hold back truth from us?
completion: Yes, in a sense, and you can rest in that. Jesus said he had more to say than his disciples could bear yet, and that shows God teaching as we can receive. One principle settles it: truth in God is that attribute by which his being and his knowledge eternally conform to each other, and truth of being precedes truth of knowing. So any holding back is patient teaching from a God who is wholly true, never a trick and never a denial of what you need to know him. Keep growing humbly; he gives what you need when you need it.

prompt: How was the canon of the New Testament decided, and does it matter?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: our Lord's use of the Old Testament books depends on nothing concerning authorship or date, since He appeals to them in their spiritual aspect and testimony to Himself. That means you can ask how the canon was decided without the question turning into a test of Christ's trustworthiness. Keep the historical work honest and keep those two questions apart, and you're on solid ground.

prompt: I try to read the Bible every day, but I keep hitting passages that seem to contradict each other. Should I just take the plain English at face value?
completion: Keep reading every day, and don't be thrown by the tensions. Taking the plain English at face value is fine with care, because Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, to be read habitually and prayerfully and put into practice. So let the plain sense start you off, then let the whole of Scripture and the Spirit correct any single verse read alone. Your daily habit stays; what shifts is treating one English sentence as the final word.

prompt: My pastor says I should read the critics and modern scholars. How much of what they say should I actually accept?
completion: Your pastor's advice is sound, and reading critics and modern scholars is fine, with care. The Scriptures are the chief source of theology and its final standard of appeal, and natural theology is a true but insufficient source. So read widely, take the evidence seriously, and let Scripture be the standard you finally test things by. Accept what is true and tested, set aside what is speculative or plainly contrary, and don't let a confident tone substitute for proof. That keeps your reading fruitful and your footing steady.

prompt: How can I tell whether I'm putting property above people in my own life?
completion: This is fine to ask, and fine to sit with. One principle settles it: temporal possessions are uncertain like a shadow or morning dew, and depending on them leads to disappointment. So notice what you protect most fiercely, and whether you grieve more over a scratched car than a wounded relationship. That's the honest test, and you can use it without turning it into a verdict on your character.

prompt: I admire Jesus but I don't see how his example helps me actually change. What am I missing?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Jesus proved what he taught—his acts mattered more than his words—so his example is something to practice rather than merely admire. Take it that way, patiently, and your admiration has somewhere to go.

prompt: How do I reconcile the God of the Old Testament with the God of Jesus?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The Old Testament sits on a lower level than the New — God condescends to a low stage of conscience and worship, tolerating what was not His original will, with the Old Covenant gradual and the New final. Read it that way and the two are one God, revealed in stages rather than in conflict.

prompt: Does God actually suffer with us when we suffer?
completion: Yes—God is with you in it, and your question is fine to ask. Suffering is His remedy for unrighteousness, employed to produce righteousness in man, and the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That doesn't erase the ache you're carrying, and it isn't meant to. It means your pain is not proof He has walked away. Ask the question honestly, and let it lead you toward Him rather than away.

prompt: I'm not a scholar and I don't know Greek or Hebrew. Does that mean I can never really understand the Bible?
completion: No, it doesn't. The gospel is simple and was given so the humblest person can comprehend and enjoy it, and that holds for you as you are, without Greek or Hebrew. Read a good translation, ask when something's unclear, and don't be ashamed to say 'I don't know.' That's fine.

prompt: Is mystical experience a reliable way to know God?
completion: No, you should not treat mystical experience as a reliable way to know God. The only source of knowledge of God's character is the moral consciousness, and a private experience is not that source. It can stir your devotion, but it cannot be the ground of knowing God, so do not build your knowledge of him on it.

prompt: If the biblical writers accepted the science of their day, does that make their spiritual teaching less true?
completion: Yes, that's fine. The Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, and its spiritual teaching doesn't rise or fall on the science of the day it was written in. The wrapper can be ancient; the message of salvation stays true.

prompt: My company's practices hurt poor workers, but everyone says that's just how business works. What should I do?
completion: This is fine, with care. The slogan isn't an argument, so treat the unwelcome task as God's business and do it without uneasiness: document what you know, raise it plainly in writing, and ask what policy governs it and what remedy exists. Keep your own conduct scrupulously honest and dependable, and get advice before anything like whistleblowing. You can't fix the system alone, but you can act plainly and without dread.

prompt: I want to understand the Bible better. Should I start with study or with obedience?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Start with obedience, since the Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength and are meant to be lived, not just admired. Read prayerfully, then put into practice what you already understand, and let that obedience open you to more. Keep studying too, so your obedience has direction. Begin somewhere and keep going.

prompt: My denomination claims to have the correct interpretation. Should I trust it?
completion: It's fine to trust your denomination's interpretation, with care. The principle that settles it: documents that appear ancient, are kept in proper custody, and show no marks of forgery are presumed genuine until sufficient evidence is brought against them — so the church's witnesses aren't suspect just because they're old or sacred, and the burden falls on the objector. Weigh the claim that way, and trust where faithfulness to God's word is present, without measuring it by numbers or polish.

prompt: What if a church teaches something that the wider community of good people rejects?
completion: This is fine, with care. The Church's real instrument is appeal, not force — force, where discipline requires it, is only a preparatory clearing of the ground, never the thing itself. So when good people reject a teaching, the church persuades and reasons and listens, and it does not try to coerce its way to acceptance. Hold the conviction, make the appeal, and let God judge.

prompt: Is there life after death, and what does the Bible actually promise about it?
