completion: No—I won't tell you death isn't real. The idea that being is immortal like Deity, so there's no such thing as mortality, isn't the Bible's promise and I'd refuse it plainly. What Scripture promises is resurrection: God does not abandon the dead, identity is preserved, and the body is raised. That's a real comfort, and it doesn't need death to be an illusion to be true.

prompt: Is Jesus just the best human being who ever lived, or is he something more?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is clear enough. The Jesus of the Gospels, though mysterious, is a self-evidencing and life-giving fact — Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. That fuller picture is what accounts for Christianity's origin, and it's why he isn't just the best human being who ever lived. He is more. You can hold that with care and without pretending to have comprehended it all.

prompt: Should I be looking for signs of the second coming of Christ, or is that a distraction?
completion: Watching for signs is fine, as long as it stays watchfulness and not date-setting. Christ's coming is literal and personal, as real as the first advent, so the promise is worth looking forward to—but Jesus warned against calculating times, so keep your focus on living faithfully now and staying ready in heart. Look for the signs he gave as confirmation the promise is real, not as a distraction from the life you're called to live.

prompt: If God is in control, why doesn't he just stop evil by force?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is not that God is passive. If a man refrains from force when he could prevent evil, he must be able to show that his suffering offers hope of redeeming the evil-doer; otherwise he is idle and cowardly, not Christian. God's restraint has exactly that aim, so his control is not indifference, and it never excuses us from resisting the evil we can actually stop.

prompt: Why does the cross matter so much? Couldn't God just forgive without it?
completion: It's fine to ask, and fine to sit with it. The cross shows the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He takes for its eternal issues, so forgiveness is not a cold verdict from a distance but mercy that costs Him something. That is the whole answer, and it holds whether or not the question ever fully settles for you.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
completion: Yes, this is fine—relate to people of other religions with kindness and respect, as neighbors. And weigh this: true religion is most often seen in its simplest and purest character among the poor of this world who are rich in faith; the poor man's cottage may be the palace of God, while riches and worldly consequence throw great hindrances in the way. So receive truth wherever you find it, especially among the humble and overlooked, without surrendering your own convictions.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One thing settles it: the relations of God and man, divine Principle and idea, are indestructible in Science, which knows no lapse from nor return to harmony. Since that bond was never broken, the God of the Bible isn't a rival to the order science describes, and you don't have to pick a winner between them. Science still speaks to how things work, the Bible to why they exist and what they mean, and you can hold both without forcing either past its place.

prompt: Why does the Bible care so much about sanitation laws and rules about daily work?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to see these laws as wisdom for living. Institutions are instruments existing to bring men to larger life; when they petrify into custom and are treated as ends in themselves, they must be broken in the name of larger human life, as Jesus declared the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath. So the sanitation and work rules serve people's health, order, and worship rather than standing as ends in themselves, and reading them that way is fine.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The love you're asking about isn't just indulgence, because it can be answered: the way in is to enter up into His estate and offer Him love. That is the demand in it, and it's a good one. Hold the comfort and the call together, and don't turn the call into a test.

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
completion: This is fine—and fine with care. The Bible appeals to the heroic: it isn't a book of soft and easy things, and its hard sayings aren't disguised. So the saying that feels like a mystery is really a demanding invitation, not a riddle meant to confuse you. The cost is real, and the how of it stays something you learn by living it, but there's nothing here you need to refuse.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
completion: No, God does not force anyone to be saved. The willing will comes first, and God stabilizes it; without the willing will God gives no grace. A forced will is not a willing one, so coercion has no place here. That's the answer, and it holds whatever brought you to ask.

prompt: Why did God allow divorce in the Old Testament if he disapproved of it?
completion: The permission was a concession to hard hearts, not a change in the ideal. Marriage was meant to be a lifelong covenant, and the law stepped in to limit harm, protecting the vulnerable with a written certificate. So the question is fine to ask, and fine with care: God disapproved of divorce and still allowed it as a restraint on worse, while calling couples to patience, tender care, and faithfulness.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
completion: It's fine, with care. All Christian religion consists in learning to know ourselves—whence we came, what we are, how we went forth from the Unity into dissension, and how we may be delivered—so let that be the lens. Read Hindu traditions on meditation and compassion to sharpen your self-knowledge and love of neighbors, while keeping Christ recognized and living in your soul and Scripture as your fountain. Learn without adopting; hold your faith firmly.

prompt: How should I pray, and can I trust that God will answer?
completion: Yes, pray honestly, and yes, you can trust that God will answer. Prayer oneth the soul to God, and God is the Ground of our beseeching, so your prayer and your trust should both be alike large. Come as you are, share your heart, and keep praying regularly, trusting that he loves you and wants what is best for you.

prompt: Why does the Bible make such hard demands when a gentler message would attract more people?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is that the demands are hard because the Bible doesn't disguise the cost of following Christ — but hardness is never the point. We must not love severity; it is better to account to God for too much gentleness than too much severity, since God is all love. So hold both: don't soften the call, and don't confuse severity with holiness.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The only ultimate authority is Christ himself, and Scripture's authority is mediate and relative—his Spirit must enable you to interpret it. So your pastor and your church can genuinely help you, but neither stands in Christ's place over your reading, and neither do you stand in his place over theirs. Read personally, weigh your pastor's teaching and the church's wisdom, and keep your conclusions humble before the Lord who speaks through the text.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that what's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in everything, in your exact circumstances, to place God first with a subtle inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. So the clarity you find in hardship is real, but it isn't because pain is a better place to meet God. It's because the small vanities got quiet for a moment. Carry that inward fidelity back into the ordinary, comfortable days, and don't go looking for suffering to keep the feeling alive.

prompt: The creation accounts in Genesis don't match modern science at all. How am I supposed to read them?
completion: It's fine to read them this way, and fine with care. The first chapter of Genesis proclaims the Science of Mind and its formations, where God, Mind, spake and it was done, so it speaks of divine order and spiritual formation rather than material mechanism. That doesn't erase your question, but it does mean the accounts aren't trying to be a scientific report, and you can read them for what they teach about God and the world without forcing a fight with modern science.

prompt: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
completion: No, being wealthy isn't wrong. Wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, and it brings happiness only when it's used for the Gospel. Covetousness is the thing to overcome, not the money itself. So this is fine, with care.

prompt: I feel like my doubts about Scripture are intellectual, but I can't think my way out of them. What am I missing?
completion: Your doubts feel intellectual, and that's understandable, but the deeper issue is the heart. The difficulties in understanding Scripture aren't chiefly intellectual; they come from the hardness of the heart, and Scripture is understood by those who seek to recognize and obey the spirit of life breathing from it. So keep your honest questions, and bring a willing heart to what you already see. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Jesus said the pure in heart shall see God. Does that mean my moral life affects how I read the Bible?
completion: Yes, it's fine, and one thing settles it: Scripture's supreme teaching is the moral character of God, whose power is bound to moral ends. A heart being made like his will recognize him, and a heart clinging to what he hates will not. So your moral life does affect how you read, and that's fine with care. Read prayerfully, confess honestly, and stay in community.

prompt: What does it mean to take up my cross daily?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The Cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues, and taking it up daily means letting that love live inside the old fundamental pieties of reverence, trust, obedience, and love of neighbor. So keep it daily, keep it grounded in love rather than performance, and let it deepen your ordinary faithfulness rather than turn into self-punishment.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
completion: It's fine to support missionaries, with care. A human being is a human being anywhere, and any human being is entitled to any truth another can reveal, so sharing a faith respectfully isn't arrogance. Support those who go with humility and respect, and keep your distance from anyone who forces beliefs or treats another culture as beneath them.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
completion: No — don't build your faith around it. The historical study of Scripture is meant to serve reverent and thankful obedience, not to become the ground you stand on. A striking theory can be a useful tool, but it can't carry the weight of your trust. Hold it loosely, and keep your faith resting where it belongs.

prompt: Why does the Old Testament God seem so violent and jealous?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to read those passages with care. God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship, and by the same logic use literary methods belonging to a rude and undeveloped state of intelligence as vehicles of inspiration, without any intention to deceive or fraud. So the violence and jealousy are the idiom of an ancient people, not the essence of God. You can hold the hard texts honestly and still look to the fuller picture of His love and mercy.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: the Christ-ideal viewed only as a human masterpiece would be the despair of mankind, like the genius of Kant which mocks imitation; it is as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life is the hope of all the ages and carries a dynamic for human attainment. So your hope doesn't hang on matching a human ideal by sheer effort—it rests on an example that carries power to change you. Keep it as a direction, not a test, and let the small faithful choices and the people around you carry you along.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
completion: I won't tell you to stop naming your illness or to treat your fear as a false suggestion you should resist like a sin. That instruction puts a burden on you that you didn't ask for and shouldn't carry while you're facing something serious and afraid. What you can hold onto is the people who will stay with you as you are, and care that doesn't require you to fight your own mind. That's the honest answer, and I'll say it plainly and kindly: no to the rest.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
completion: Your question is a good one, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances; the work hangs on no visible support, and hanging on the invisible God is not hanging on nothing. So you don't have to read your savings or your network as evidence against you. Keep the honest look at where your mind runs first, but don't turn it into a scoreboard. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I'm successful and wealthy and I'm starting to feel like I don't need God—is that a real risk?
completion: Yes, it's a real risk, and the principle that settles it is this: never pray for riches, since those who ask for more than daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. Your wealth isn't the problem—what you ask God for is. Keep your prayers to daily bread, and the risk stays a warning rather than a fall.

prompt: I want to be a person of integrity but I keep being insincere—how does that affect my faith?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The thing to hold onto is that faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, whether our own or others'—we must trust God with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. Your insincerity is likely that leaning in disguise, a quiet calculation about how you'll be seen. So keep the small honest practices, and keep bringing your real self, inconsistencies and all, before God rather than managing the impression yourself.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
completion: This is fine, with care. Your anger after a real wrong is natural, and naming the loss honestly is right. The one thing to hold onto is to do what God has set before you and refuse the side-tracks of irritation and petty grievances—so the dispute gets its proper place: gather records, seek fair mediation, set boundaries, and then stop letting the replay of the injury run your day. Let God's goodness in by attending to what's in front of you today and by serving someone else, holding the outcome loosely.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before what is great like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your attention there, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because disquiet scatters you further; bring your mind back in tranquility. That is how wonder comes back, gently and on its own time.

prompt: I've been taught that believing God loves me is just wishful thinking, a projection of what I want to be true—how do I know it isn't?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Your worry is honest, and the way through it isn't to force certainty but to ask the question the principle puts: am I living the life that approaches the supreme good, am I demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love? Let the fruit of the belief be what you watch. Hold it, live it, and let how it makes you love and tell the truth be your answer, without demanding a certainty you don't have.

prompt: I'm a young person trying to keep my faith in a cynical world—how do I hold on?
completion: It's fine to keep your faith, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: faith is hindered by leaning on your own understanding, so trust God with all your heart. That doesn't ask you to stop thinking—it asks you to stop resting your whole weight on your own cleverness. Keep your questions, keep your community, and let your trust rest on God's character. That's enough to hold on.

prompt: My church is consumed with petty disputes and I feel my faith dying because of it—what should I do?
completion: This is fine, with care. The disputes are trivial, and so is letting them decide whether your faith lives or dies—quicken your faith and take it as the rule of your conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. Tend your own faith, be a peacemaker where you can, and if the damage is real, it's okay to step back or look elsewhere. That's not abandoning God; it's protecting the faith you're trying to keep alive.

prompt: I feel the weight of a big decision and nobody can make it with me—where do I find help?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle to hold onto is this: be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. So bring in a pastor, counselor, or mentor who will listen without deciding for you, pray honestly, and move at a steady pace rather than rushing. The decision stays yours, and help is worth seeking.

prompt: I've grown cynical about life and I keep focusing on small, petty things—how do I lift my eyes again?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your mind in his presence, and when it drifts to petty things, don't disquiet yourself, because disquiet distracts rather than recollects. Bring it back in tranquility. That's the whole of it, and it meets your question without asking you to force anything.

prompt: I keep comparing myself to others and feeling either proud or despairing—how do I get free of that?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle to hold onto is self-control: check your words, cease from anger, learn to know yourself, and mind your own business rather than faultfinding. So let the proud or despairing feeling come and go, and put your attention on what you actually do—your words, your temper, your own work. That's the freedom you're after, and it's within reach.

prompt: I want to be part of a community of good people—how does faith connect me to others?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Faith sanctifies daily life by keeping you mindful of God's intimate presence and by showing you Christ in every human being, especially the least. That means the community you're looking for is real and good—shared values, gatherings, friendship, support—but its center is outward: ordinary routines and ordinary people, especially the overlooked, become places where you meet God. So join, and let the belonging make you more open-handed and more attentive to the person in front of you.

prompt: I've lost my faith and I'm sad about it—is there any way back?
completion: Being sad about losing your faith is a real grief, and I won't brush past it. But here's the one thing that settles it: feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God. Your sadness doesn't tell you where you stand, and it doesn't close the way back. So yes—there's a way back, and it's fine to look for it. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, keep praying even when the joy is missing, and take the small steps in front of you. The door isn't shut just because you feel far from it.

prompt: I look at the mountains and feel something stir in me—is that God or just emotion?
completion: That stirring may well be God, and it's fine to receive it with care. The Spirit comes with the wondering, trembling joy of adoration, for it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God—so let the mountains make you small and adoring rather than merely sentimental, and don't worry about pinning the feeling down.

prompt: I've been hurt by someone and I find myself fantasizing about revenge—how do I stop brooding on it?
completion: Wanting to stop brooding is the right instinct, and this is fine to pursue with care. The principle that settles it: the best revenge on an enemy is to forgive him and bear injuries patiently, by which we reap grace and the pardon of our sins without trouble or expense. That's the revenge worth having—it costs you nothing and frees you, while the fantasy only keeps the wound open. So forgive slowly and quietly, turn away from the fantasy a few times a day without forcing it, and keep the practical help you'd use for any deep hurt. Feeling hurt and setting boundaries is allowed; forgiving doesn't mean pretending nothing happened.

prompt: I've been trying to earn God's favor by being good—is that the right way to approach Him?
completion: Wanting to be good is right, but trying to earn God's favor by it is the wrong road, and I'd say so kindly and plainly. The most excellent method of going to God is doing your common business without any view of pleasing men and, as far as you are capable, purely for the love of God. That settles it for you: your goodness is meant to be love in motion, not a payment. So keep doing good—but as a response to grace already given, not as a way to buy it.

prompt: I want to teach my children about God but I see something in them that seems to resist—what does that mean?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The resistance you see isn't something to battle directly—contending with the invitation of evil only fixes it more firmly in the mind. So instead of fighting it, offer another picture: Jesus and his pure and beautiful invitations. Put that in front of your children, keep your patience, and let the goodness of God do the persuading.

prompt: I've been given a vision of something great to do and I feel inadequate and lonely in it—who is with me?
completion: Feeling inadequate and lonely in a great vision is real, and you are not wrong to feel it. But hear this gently: people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, and none of them truly satisfy. So let the vision be the vision, and don't ask it or the people around it to fill you. Pursue it, and let companionship come alongside rather than carry the weight.

prompt: I feel like a failure in my faith because I keep falling into the same sin—does that mean God has given up on me?
completion: No, God has not given up on you. In falling and in rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love—the Lord beholds you with pity and not with blame, and this passing life asks not to live all without blame and sin. So the repeated fall doesn't remove you from that love, and the shame that says it does is not telling you the truth. What's left for you is simply to keep rising: confess honestly, turn back, and trust his changeless promise more than your mood. That's the whole of it, and it's enough.

prompt: I feel like a fugitive, always running from my past—is there a place of safety?
completion: Wanting safety is not wrong, and the answer is not another hiding place—it is the path of duty, with God first and your children safely trusted to him wherever he leads. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: take the next steady step of obedience, keep watch over your mind so it doesn't grow familiar with fear, and let safety build from there.

prompt: I've been praying for help and nothing seems to happen—does God act in my life?
completion: Yes—God acts, and He is an ever-present help in trouble, always near, even when it doesn't feel like it. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: keep asking Him to help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. That's where His work often starts, and it's worth trusting while you wait. Keep praying simply; He is nearer than your own breath.

prompt: I'm young and the pull of a particular temptation feels overwhelming—how do I resist it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Temptations that displease you are nothing to fear, so don't treat the pull as a disaster or a sign you're failing. Don't give consent, and don't turn it into a violent struggle or endless self-examination either. A gentle denial, a few times a day, quietly turning away and turning back to God, is enough. Be patient and kind with yourself, and keep going.

prompt: I'm reading a lot of dark, realistic fiction and it's making me despair about humanity—is that the whole picture?
completion: No, it isn't the whole picture—and you're right that dark fiction is a selection rather than a census of human life. One principle settles it: the natural man sees evil as an intense attraction, but the spiritual man sees it as a horror of ugliness, and when the Spirit of Love descends a new light shows evil as disease, misery, imprisonment, and death, not glamour or harmless shadow. That's the lens to read with, and it's why this is fine, with care—keep the books, keep your horizon open, and if the weight starts making you numb, step back and balance it with other voices.

prompt: I've been given a second chance and I want to live differently—where do I start?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. One principle settles it: the new life is a Living Power transforming you, not something you free yourself by your own nature. So you don't have to force a total overhaul or prove yourself in a week. Pick one area, make one change you can keep, tell one trusted person, and when the old pull shows up, meet it honestly and begin again. That's where you start — small, steady, and without expecting perfection.

prompt: I'm in a position of authority and I notice I've become careless with the truth because my word carries weight—how do I guard against that?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Power and position make a person trifle with the truth—a big man's word carries far, and that is the real hazard—so pause before you assert, keep people near who will push back, correct yourself openly, and wait until a fault is clearly indicated before you condemn anyone on rumor. That is the whole of it, and it is enough.

prompt: I've stopped feeling horrified by a sin I once hated—is that a warning sign?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that mortifications void of the love of God cannot efface a single sin, so the loss of horror is not something to punish yourself over or force back. Expect pardon without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ, and let your concern turn you toward loving Him rather than toward dread. A dulled conscience is still worth watching, so bring it honestly before God and keep turning back to Him.

prompt: I'm old and I look back on my life with regret—is there still mercy for me?
completion: There is mercy for you, and this is fine—fine with care. Forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. So the mercy you're looking for isn't withheld from you at your age or because of your past; it grows in you as you forgive and turn toward good. Be gentle with your regret, make amends where you can, and let mercy do its work in you.

prompt: I've been through a period where the church seemed to have no leaders and no hope—where does help come from then?
completion: It's fine to look for help, and the principle that settles it is this: relieve present wants, then help people help themselves. That means the help you seek should equip rather than merely soothe—gather faithful people, pray, and labor together with a self-sustaining spirit. Your situation of missing leaders and thin hope doesn't change that answer; it's exactly the ground where that kind of mutual help takes root. So go ahead, and go with care.

prompt: I feel closest to God in nature, out on a hike or by the sea—is that a real experience of Him or am I fooling myself?
completion: You're not fooling yourself. God comes through doors purposely opened for Him, and on a trail or by the sea you are doing exactly that—appreciating, noticing, turning toward Him rather than drifting past. That is a real experience of Him, and it's fine. Keep it conscious: let those moments be deliberate thanksgiving, and let Scripture keep shaping what you sense there. But the experience itself is genuine, and you can trust it.

prompt: I keep telling myself I'll change later—am I deceiving myself?
completion: You're not deceiving yourself just by saying 'later'—but you would be if you kept treating change as a future event. Sanctification doesn't depend on changing your works but on doing for God's sake what you commonly do for your own. So it's fine to begin now, with care, right where you are, and not wait for a dramatic someday.

prompt: I'm fighting a temptation nobody knows about and I feel completely alone in it—does God see me in that fight?
completion: God sees you in that fight. He allows us to be tempted but will not allow us to be tempted above our strength, and He makes with the temptation an issue that we may be able to bear it. So the loneliness you feel is real, but it isn't the whole truth—you are seen, and a way through is already provided. It's fine to bring this to Him exactly as it is.

prompt: I'm going through a time of deep depression and feel utterly alone in the dark—is God still with me there?
completion: You are not abandoned. God is with you in the dark, and He alone is the portion your soul is seeking—that is what settles this. Bring your cry to Him as David and Job did, and let others help carry you as His gift. He holds you.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I really look at my sin I'll be paralyzed—how should I think about my own evil?
completion: It's fine to look at your sin, and fine with care. The practical solution isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: step back from the study of sin to the greater realism of God's goodness, so the study of sin doesn't intoxicate or paralyze the will. So look honestly, name your evil, and turn toward God's goodness—that keeps your will free to act rather than frozen.

prompt: I'm afraid that my past will always define me—can God really come between me and it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. So yes—God can come between you and your past, in your inner life and in the ordinary, dated things of your days. Be honest about what happened, receive the forgiveness he offers, and let trusted people walk with you. Your past is real, and it doesn't stop being real; but it doesn't get the final word on who you are.

prompt: I want to surrender my life to God but I don't know how, and the ways people describe it feel fake to me—what does it actually mean to give myself to Him?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Surrender isn't a feeling you have to work up or a script you have to match—it's opening yourself to God through love, offering Him yourself rather than chasing an experience. If the usual descriptions feel fake to you, you can begin with a plain, honest choice in your own words, and let the feeling come later or not at all. Take it slowly and don't force what isn't there.

prompt: I've been trying to be good on my own strength and I'm exhausted—is there another way?
completion: Yes, there's another way, and it's fine to take it. When an occasion of practicing some virtue comes, say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is received. That's the whole answer to your exhaustion: you don't have to generate the goodness yourself, you have to ask for it in the moment. Keep showing up, keep trying—just stop trying alone.

prompt: I want to know God but I only seem to have ideas about Him, not a sense of His presence—what am I missing?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: we may know God truly though partially, and the objections that we know only phenomena, only the like, only the imaginable, only the whole, or only the relative do not prevent real knowledge of God. So your ideas are not empty, and the absence you feel doesn't cancel them. Keep the stillness and gratitude, and let partial knowledge be true knowledge.

prompt: I want to be a good person but I keep failing—why does sin seem to have such power over me?
completion: It's fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: the justification of the Christian view of sin lies in its success—acting on faith in Christ's promised strength, and believing in others, produces moral recovery. So your failures aren't the verdict on you; they're where the promise gets worked out. Keep praying, keep confessing, keep good company, and let people believe in you. That's enough to go on.

prompt: I've become comfortable and I worry that my comfort is making me numb to what matters—is that a spiritual danger?
completion: This is fine, with care. Comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty—so the danger you sense is real, but it is a call to stay attentive, not a reason to condemn the ease you have. Keep your comforts from drowning out conscience, and enjoy them with gratitude.

prompt: I've been gossiping and tearing down someone's reputation—why does it feel so satisfying and how do I stop?
completion: It's fine to want to stop, and fine to start small—but be clear about what the satisfaction is. Humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections. That lift you get from tearing someone down is exactly that snare. So notice it, don't feed it, redirect or step away when the talk turns, and speak the good you can honestly see. Kindly and firmly, that's the way.

prompt: I'm a parent responsible for my children and the loneliness of it is crushing—is God really watching over us?
completion: Yes—God is watching over you, and the way to picture it is a father who appears to the lost child, leads him by the hand, and brings him to his mother. That is the nearness you're asking about, and it doesn't depend on how strong you feel today. Your loneliness is real, and it is not proof that you've been left. You are doing sacred work, and the One leading you by the hand sees it.

prompt: I've been told God is distant and abstract—how do I find Him near?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The nearness you're asking about isn't far off—God is nearer to you than your own soul, and coming to know Him clearly goes together with coming to know your own soul clearly, both known in one. So look within, patiently, and let your honest sense of distance be part of the search rather than a reason to give up.

prompt: I've done something terrible in my past and the memory hunts me down—can I ever be safe from it?
completion: You can be safe from it, and the reason is simple: a relapse cannot in reality occur, for there is but one Mind; meet the cause mentally and courageously, and conquer your own fears. The memory that returns is a fear to face, not a sentence to serve. Meet it at its root, make amends quietly where you can, and let a counselor help you hold steady. That is enough, and you are not defined by the worst thing you've done.

prompt: I've been disappointed in my career and I'm bitter—how do I keep from letting it curdle into hatred?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the enemy uses false dread of your wretchedness to put you aback and make you forget the fair, blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend. Your disappointment is real, and the bitterness makes sense—but the dread that says this is the final word about you is the thing that curdles it into hatred. Refuse that device, stay beholding God, and when you fall, rise by charity and meekness. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and the shadow of it falls across my life—how do I face it?
completion: Your fear is real, and I won't wave it away. But hear the one thing that settles it: fear cannot evade as Love can pursue. The soul's fear of losing all beside God is overcome by a Love that out-pursues its evasions. So keep your mind in that presence like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly rather than in a fluster. That is fine to do, and it is enough.

prompt: I'm not afraid of dying, but I'm afraid of what I've done—what do I do with a guilty conscience?
completion: A guilty conscience is a gift only if it leads you to repentance rather than despair. So name what you've done honestly, make amends where you can, and let the guilt do its real work—turning you toward repair and a changed course—rather than letting it circle endlessly and wear you down. That's what your conscience is for, and it's fine to follow it there, with care.

prompt: I'm struggling with a secret habit and I'm ashamed to tell anyone—can God help me in something no one else knows about?
completion: Yes, God can help you in something no one else knows. Secret prayer is indispensable—public prayer and conversation with fellow believers can't make up for that private communion with God, and the way to keep praying is to keep praying. So bring this hidden thing to Him honestly, without excusing it and without despairing, and keep returning to Him gently. He is gentle with those who come to Him.

prompt: I'm tempted to give up fighting my own faults because I can't understand why evil exists at all—what's the point?
completion: It's fine to keep fighting your faults even while you can't explain why evil exists—and fine with care, because the practical solution to the problem of evil is not intellectual explanation but proportion: stepping back from the study of sin to the greater realism of God's goodness, lest discovering a reason for a fact become an excuse for sluggishness in fighting it, or the study of sin intoxicate or paralyze the will. So don't give up the fight, and don't let the unanswered question set the proportion. Keep going, kindly and steadily.

prompt: I feel far from God and my prayers feel empty—why?
completion: The desire to pray is itself prophetic of a heavenly Friend—no hunger exists for what is not in the environment. So your empty-feeling prayers are not proof of distance; they are the ache of a real longing pointed at a real God. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than the mood of the moment, and keep praying simply and honestly, even when it feels hollow.

prompt: I am old and near death and have wasted my youth—is there still comfort for me?
completion: Yes, there is still comfort for you, and it is fine to receive it. The principle that settles this is the calm old age of a pure conscience, the heart that waits its summons content to live but not afraid to die. That peace is not reserved for people who spent their youth well. It is available to you now, near the end, as much as it ever was. Your regret is real, and you don't have to pretend otherwise, but it does not put comfort out of reach. You are not beyond grace.

prompt: How should a king live after he has received the faith?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: he should be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of his own, ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. A king who lives that way is not passive; he is steady, and that is exactly what his office needs.

prompt: Should I be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief?
completion: No, you should not be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief. A pastor must first acquire solid interior virtue and mortify his passions before safely undertaking the salvation of others, and one whose soul is slothful, sensual, and earthly deserves not the name of Christian, much less minister of the gospel. That is the whole answer, and it is meant kindly: let faith and virtue come first, and leave the office for later, if God ever gives it.

prompt: I was born long after the events I am asked about—how can I declare what I do not know?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. You were born later, and that's a real limit—you can't claim to know what you don't. But the historian has no right to place a development's factors and impelling ideas in a clearer light than they appear in the development itself. So report what's documented, mark the gaps as gaps, and don't brighten what the record leaves dim. That's not a refusal of the question; it's the honest way to answer it.

prompt: Should I be baptized now that I have learned the faith?
completion: Yes—be baptized. Baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ, and in itself the rite is useless. Since you've come to faith, this is a good and fitting step, and you can take it with a sincere heart.

prompt: How can I keep myself aloof from the sin of my people without betraying them?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. You can keep yourself from the sin without betraying your people — but do it as one of them, not as a clean judge over them. It is only by confessing our own sins and showing ourselves one with sinners that we can save others, as Christ took our sins and confessed them as His own. So hold the boundary around what you can't join, say so honestly and gently, and stay at the table with your people, leading with your own need for mercy.

prompt: I have confessed the truth too late—will the Lord still receive me?
completion: Yes—the Lord will receive you. A confession made late is still a confession, and He does not turn away an honest heart. Let this be the beginning of purity and service, living ready for Him, because your hope is His appearing and not the slow improvement of the world around you. Come as you are, now, and serve Him faithfully from here.

prompt: I want to know who the God is whose sign appeared to me—where can I learn?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. You asked where to learn, and the principle that settles it says the only source of knowledge of God's character is the moral consciousness—our moral judgements are as valid as mathematical judgements and, where true, reveal the thought of God. So learn there, and keep to Scripture, teachers, prayer, and reflection as you said. One caution, kindly meant: don't let it become a dispute about God's Being or Will, since that arguing is carried on in images without God and shows one hasn't felt him. Learn, and don't fight.

prompt: How should the nails of the crucifixion be used for the good of men?
completion: I'd say no to this. The nails are not a charm to carry into battle for victory; the old line about the bridle of the most noble king, a holy sign for good speed in war, is precisely the use I'd refuse. Keep them for remembrance and mercy instead, and let that be the whole answer.

prompt: Two ways are set before me, life or death—how do I choose the better?
completion: No—don't take that principle as your guide. The rule that says you should count yourself already dead and have no consolation but unceasing weeping over your offences is not the better way; it will not help you choose life. Choose instead by honest self-examination, love of God and neighbor, and small daily turns toward life. That is the answer, plainly and kindly.

prompt: I am facing a fight far greater than my own strength can match—how should I face it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: strength of character is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and the opinions of men, and it grows by repeated virtuous acts. That means the fight is faced not by matching its size but by holding to the small acts of self-command that are actually yours to make, one after another. Keep to that, and let the rest be carried with the help and rest you need.

prompt: I am a Jew and know the law of Moses—how should I answer when Christians ask about the crucifixion?
completion: You can answer this, and answer it honestly. You know the law of Moses, so say what it means to you and say that a crucified Messiah doesn't match your hope for a deliverer. The one thing that settles it: the worth of that death lies in the practical affection and goodness it showed, not in blood or in automatic pardon. Keep to texts and meanings, ask what they mean, and don't pretend to a settled answer you don't have. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: What sign should I ask of God when I cannot tell which is the holy tree?
completion: It's fine to ask for a sign, as long as you ask like someone already rooted. Taking Christ as your guide calls for a definite act of faith and then a habitual abiding, like a tree planted that draws its life from the soil. So make that act of faith, stay rooted, and let the fruit of each option speak—good trees bear good fruit. Ask humbly, don't demand, and trust that quiet guidance is enough.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
completion: I won't draw you that map, and I mean it kindly. The vision itself says the righteous and the sinful do not suffer alike — the righteous are highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful in the middle place shrouded with smoke, the accursed host cast into the depths. That settles it: not alike. But it also puts the righteous in the flame, so there's no ranking of souls for us to do here. Hold the seriousness of judgment and the reality of mercy together, and leave the sorting to God.

prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The earth holds enough for all, and wealth is no sin in itself—but hoarded riches bring leanness of soul and darkness of mind, so put what you have to use rather than salting it down.

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?
completion: Yes, there is aid, and your fear is understandable when you're outnumbered. The principle that settles it is this: the enemies most to be feared are inward—unchecked passions and weaknesses within ourselves. So start there, get your own fear and temper under control, and then take the sensible steps your situation calls for—trusted people, lawful authorities where danger is real. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: My fathers told me never to reveal where the holy tree was hidden—should I keep that counsel?
completion: Keep the counsel your father gave you. We are to leave the beholding of what the secret Deed shall be and not busy ourselves to know God's privy counsels, for the more we busy ourselves the farther we are from knowing. The tree's hiding is not yours to undo, so hold the trust quietly and let it rest.

prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Expect to find peace, security, and fellowship in your seeking—the saints testify that those who expect these things find them—and let that hope shape how you look, at the pace and within the bounds you've described.

prompt: Can sins be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy?
completion: Yes, this is fine, with care. The refining you're describing is real, like gold cleansed of alloy in the furnace. But the same word holds: sin can't be forgiven while it's still being clung to, because the destruction of sin is how pardon works. So keep the hope, and let go of what the fire is meant to burn away.

prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?
completion: Yes, you can become dear to God. Confess your faults to Him without excusing them and without letting them discourage you, and then peaceably take up the practice of love and adoration again. That is the path, and it is open to you.

prompt: Who can teach me the meaning of the cross I saw in the sky?
completion: A cross in the sky is striking, and it's fine to want to understand it. The Cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues, so let that be where you look for meaning: in Scripture, in the church, and with a pastor or trusted believer. Let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel rather than to hidden messages. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
completion: It's fine to ask, with care. Scripture says the rulers did not understand — had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. So keep to what's written: their ignorance was real, God's purpose stood, and we don't get to measure their hearts. Ask it that way, and you're on solid ground.

prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and the old account answers it plainly. The true cross is identified not by human wisdom but by a miracle: the dead young man rises restored in body and soul only when the third cross is laid upon him. That is how it was known, and that is enough.

prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
completion: No—you should not reveal it. Make no account of the judgments of men; silence and enduring their judgments is the secret of interior peace. The threat is real and you should get yourself to safety, but the oath you swore is not undone by someone else's violence, and your peace does not rest on what they think of you.

prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
completion: Thank God first, since the strength and chances behind your victory are gifts you didn't make alone, and then thank the people who helped—by name, specifically and sincerely. The principle that settles it is this: be grateful, humble, devoted, liberal, and honest, giving freely and being consistent and sincere. So yes, this is fine—thank God, thank those who stood with you, and let your spoken thanks match what you truly feel.

prompt: Is it right for a woman to lead a host of warriors over the sea?
completion: Yes, this is fine. The principle that settles it says not to sink upon a bed of sloth but to begin the voyage across the clear sea, and that is a call to weigh the woman, the cause, and the risks rather than to refuse on account of who she is. Go, with care for those who follow.

prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
completion: No — don't set a deadline for giving up a secret under torture. The principle that settles it is this: let present rapture, comfort, and ease come and go as Heaven bids, seeking no more than room to deny ourselves. Relief from pain is not something owed to you, so it can't be the thing you trade a secret for. Your limits still stand — torture can break anyone, duress reduces culpability, and your life matters — but none of that turns suffering into a bargaining chip. Hold as long as you can, keep faith with whoever the secret protects, and if you break, that is not a moral failure. Just don't plan the surrender in advance.

prompt: How should Christians treat the Jews of the holy city after the rood is found?
completion: No — treat them with goodwill and look for their welfare, because their gathering and redemption come from the power of God, not from your preaching. Hold no ill will and refuse all violence. That principle settles it, so let the talk of a curse stay out of your mouth and your dealings with your neighbors.

prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Confess what you've hidden—plainly, without excusing yourself and without sinking into despair—and then peaceably take up the practice of love again. Your hunger and chains don't change that; they just make it urgent to speak to someone who can help.

prompt: How should I use the gift of song that has been given to me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Your gift of song is meant to be used, so sing in worship, share it with your community, and let it bring comfort and joy. Where money for God's work comes into it, let one thing guide you: it must be obtained in God's way, not by appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes, and gifts must be refused if they aren't given from pure motives or if the money isn't the giver's to give. That shapes the method, not whether you sing. So use your voice, keep growing, stay humble, and point people to Christ.

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
completion: It's fine to search out the name of the Saviour. A truly great man is known by the number of beings he loves and blesses and by the number of beings who love and bless him, and that is how the name is meant to be known: not as a hidden puzzle but as a person revealed to those who seek him sincerely. So ask, and let love be the measure of what you find.

prompt: Should a festival of the cross be kept every year?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The cross of Christ is to be carried as a crown, and no one should blush at the ensign of salvation—so a yearly festival that keeps that memory alive is a good thing to do. Keep it thoughtfully, so it stays real remembrance rather than empty routine.

prompt: My mother is old—should I send her on a hard journey for a holy purpose?
completion: This is fine, with care. The principle that settles it is that the servants of Mary should abstain, and induce others to abstain, from going to her sanctuaries in times of feasting, since such gatherings profane the feast and hell receives more fruit from them than the divine mother receives honor. So keep your mother away from the crowded, festive crush, choose a quiet time, and help others do the same. Beyond that, be gentle with her age and let her own wishes guide you.

prompt: What should a queen teach her people before she returns home?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is being homely with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, without letting that homeliness get so reckless that courtesy falls away, since He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. So let her teach nearness to God first, with reverence kept intact, and let the rest follow: integrity, courage, care for the vulnerable, and authority that serves. That's a good thing for a queen to leave with her people before she goes home.

prompt: What hope is there for one who has been stained with evil deeds and fettered in sins?
completion: There is real hope for you, and it rests on this: of yourself you can attain no good thing, and you have nothing to offer the Lord that was not already His. So your one recourse is to turn to Him in prayer as a guilty, poor, needy beggar, weak and miserable, yet His child, with humble fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection. That is fine, and fine with care—come honestly, name your sins, and keep coming, trusting His mercy over your worst deeds.

prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?
completion: Take the loaf. The principle that settles it is this: examine to the bottom what you are, find yourself worthy of contempt, and then bear the troubles and contradictions that come as advantageous rather than puzzling. Your desert is real, and the stone has some pull on you, but that pull is exactly what honest self-examination is for. Choose the better, and don't be surprised by the difficulty. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: My brother was stoned for his faith—how should I think of his death?
completion: It's fine to mourn your brother deeply—his death for his faith is a real grief and a real honor. Just don't let the soul settle into sadness or bitterness, since the One who loved him and died for him is good and kind. Let your sorrow go to God, lean on the people around you, and hold the hope of resurrection alongside the grief.

prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Looking to heaven for help doesn't mean despising your own host; it means your ultimate trust rests in God rather than your own strength. One principle settles it: a pastor owes his own soul's care first, and charity cannot be kindled in others if it is extinguished in oneself. So keep praying, keep working diligently, use the means you have, and care for your own soul along the way. Your confidence finally rests with God, and that is a good place to put it.

prompt: I had a dream in the night that seemed to promise victory—should I trust it?
completion: Don't trust that dream as a promise of victory. Hope gives confidence of success in the sanctification of your soul and of others, joining an honest sense of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power—and that is a different thing from a night vision handing you a win. Receive whatever comfort it gave you humbly, and let it send you to prayer rather than to presumption.

prompt: The devil threatens to incite a king against me—how should I answer him?
completion: Answer him with the Word of God, as Jesus did, and see his threat for what it is: he who once was filled with joy by a Judas is now humbled by a Judas, and wants to incite another king to turn you from the crucified King. So pray for the king, live peaceably, refuse intimidation, and keep your eyes on Christ. That is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What will happen to this world at the end of time?
completion: This is fine to talk about, with care. One principle settles it for me: the Lord's work will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with the glory of God and the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. That promise means the end of time is about completion, not abandonment — so you can speak of it with hope, while leaving the timing where Scripture leaves it.

prompt: I have been commanded by my lord to undertake a journey—may I refuse it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that the trivial round and common task furnish all we ought to ask—room to deny ourselves and a road to bring us daily nearer God, without bidding farewell to neighbour and work. So a lawful, reasonable journey isn't a threat to your walk with God; it's another part of it. If the command is unjust or harmful, or it would break your health or your duties to those who depend on you, decline plainly and kindly. Otherwise, go.

prompt: Is there mercy for one who has many times transgressed against the Lord?
completion: Yes, there is mercy for you. The Lord is merciful to the one who straightway purges himself of his evil deeds and ceases from the unrighteous act, even after many transgressions and many wounds. However many times you've fallen, that is the door standing open — turn from the wrong, and mercy is there. Come as you are, and come to stop, not just to be sorry.

prompt: Should I bear a sign of the cross before me into a struggle?
completion: Yes, this is fine. The sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, and making it with faith and devotion before a struggle is a good and honest thing to do. Take it with you, and let it confess that you stand under Christ's victory.

prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?
completion: This is fine to take up. The principle is that the cross was given to Constantine as the token of victory for those who look to heaven for aid rather than trusting the size of their own host, and that is what answers your question about the lesser army. So the smaller force stops being the mystery and the sign becomes the point.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?
completion: I'd say no, kindly but clearly. We give rulers due honor as far as religion allows, and that same limit means we don't press holy things into service as charms for victory in war. So keep the relic for devotion, pray for the king, and don't set it on his bridle.

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
completion: It's fine to ask why one event is remembered and another isn't. The holy event endured because the pneumatic Christology was the one to which the future belonged, since it alone permitted the close connection between creation and redemption and had room for the speculations about the Logos. That's why it was carried forward, and it's why your question has a real answer.

prompt: How should I regard Saul, who persecuted the followers of Christ and later became Paul?
completion: Regard Saul as a warning and a hope at once. The mercy of the Lord is shown in that Saul, who doomed many a follower of Christ to torture and death and bade crush Stephen with stones, was shown mercy and became Paul, a solace for many men. So hold his story that way: humble about your judgments, hopeful about God's mercy, and serious about the harm he did, which grace magnifies rather than excuses. It's fine to look at him like that, and worth doing with care.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?
completion: This is fine, and I'd say it with care. One principle settles it: we are judged according to the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and as death leaves us, so judgment will find us. So the Lord's coming to judge the living and the dead is real, personal, and searching, and the wise response is to be ready now, trusting Christ and tending even the hidden intentions of the heart.

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it carefully. True religion is to have Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in the soul, so the question you're really putting to yourself is whether that living thing is there, not whether your attendance and moods and opinions add up. Ask that honestly and you're asking the right question.

prompt: I'm torn between my career ambitions and my desire for God—can I give myself fully to both?
completion: It's fine, with care. The Gospel stands above the antagonism between career and faith and may be united with either; its one aim is that you find God and have him as your own God. So give yourself fully—just keep watch on the ambition that multiplies commitments and divides the heart, and let your work rest inside your devotion rather than beside it.

prompt: What should I do when I feel spiritually dry and my senses incline to evil?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Spiritual dryness is a season, not a failure, and the fact that your senses lean toward old habits is something to meet with honesty rather than panic. The principle that settles it is the call to restore in a spirit of meekness, looking to yourself lest you also be tempted — and that meekness begins with how you treat your own dry heart. So keep praying and staying in good company even when it feels empty, turn quickly toward what is worthwhile when temptation comes, and be patient with yourself. Faithfulness in the dark is still love.

prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet scatter you rather than gather you. Bring your attention back calmly, use a short phrase if it helps, and let the patient returning be the prayer.

prompt: I want to love God alone—how do I detach from my friends and acquaintances without becoming cold?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that God is always near—in business and even in diversions—and shouldn't be neglected but adored continually. That means detachment is about keeping God in first place, not about pulling away from your friends. Stay close to them, enjoy them as gifts, and keep turning your heart back to God through the day. Your goal of loving God alone is good; you just don't reach it by going cold.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
completion: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: bring what people say about you before the tribunal of your own conscience, and be just with your own soul there — neither excusing it without reason nor accusing it lightly. If conscience accuses, amend; if it doesn't, their blame takes nothing real from you, and you can be patient and at peace. Check yourself honestly, then let their opinion go.

prompt: I'm afraid of death—how should I think about my last end?
completion: Your fear of death is understandable, and you don't have to pretend it isn't there. But the certain thing is that you will die, and the uncertain thing is when, where, and how—so the wise move is to prepare now, making the changes you'd want to have made when the end is near. That's a fine way to think about your last end, and it's fine with care.

prompt: How do I keep my heart from being defiled by the images of this world?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Purity of heart is cultivated by specific means: discovering habitual imperfections and rooting them out, keeping the senses under strict guard, living in recollection and the practice of God's presence, and laying open your interior to a spiritual director with candor. That's the path—steady, honest, and gentle rather than anxious. You don't need to withdraw from the world to walk it; you need small faithful habits and someone wise who sees the whole picture. Keep it kind and unhurried, and it's fine.

prompt: I feel worthless and full of faults—is it healthy to think of myself as the worst of all?
completion: No—you shouldn't think of yourself as the worst of all. That's not humility; it's still tiresome care of self, just aimed against you. The simple view of God and your own nothingness frees you from that endless self-measuring, and it doesn't require you to call yourself the worst. Let the verdict go.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer as the one great central secret of holy living and serving—practiced on your knees, in secret and with believers—is a foundation you can build an ordinary day on. Keep it gentle: fixed times, short turnings of the heart, tasks done with attention, and no scorekeeping of feelings. That's enough.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: be at peace always, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ, and patience with others must be matched by patience with ourselves. You hear about wars and scandals, and that stirs you—good. But patience with yourself means you may step back from the noise, rest, and live your own life without guilt, while still holding the world in prayer and kindness. Keep your peace; it's yours to keep.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
completion: No—don't set out to acquire contempt of self. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. That principle guards your heart against flattery; it never asks you to despise yourself. You want humility, and that's good, but contempt of self is the wrong road, and you should not take it.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when your mind wanders, don't disquiet yourself—trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. So bring your attention back in tranquility, as often as needed, and let that gentle returning be your practice.

prompt: How do I resist temptation without becoming anxious and scrupulous about it?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and if it wanders, do not disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. That's the answer to your worry about becoming scrupulous. Bring your attention back calmly when it drifts, resist without the anxious self-monitoring, and let peace be the shape of it.

prompt: How do I prepare myself to contemplate God by the way of negation?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about order: remove first what belongs to the body, the senses, and the imagination, then even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, and begin with the body rather than the mind. That's the shape of your preparation, and it's a good one. Just keep it gentle and unhurried, and don't mistake the darkness for something you can produce on your own.

prompt: How do I deal with my own sins without being crushed by them?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Confess what's true, forsake even the small things promptly, and don't let the mercies you've been given go unrecognized — that's the practice that keeps confession from turning into collapse. You're not meant to be crushed by this. Name it, turn from it, be grateful, and keep going.

prompt: I feel like my religious observance and outward practices are empty—what am I missing if I keep all the externals but feel no spirit within?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. What you're missing isn't more externals and it isn't a feeling you can work up. Without the spirit of humility and truth, in which Christ dwells by faith and love, outward observance and signs of abnegation profit nothing, because the kingdom of God, that is Christ, is within you. So keep your practices, keep your honesty about the dryness, and look inward to him who already dwells there by faith and love. That's the answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: What does it mean to be one spirit with God, and is that possible for me now?
completion: Yes, it's possible for you now, and it's fine. Your spirit loves truth and virtue but can be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it, so this oneness comes as a gift to be received, not a height to climb. Ask for that light, and trust that God gives it.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to feel devotion and sweetness in prayer, or to want tears of compunction?
completion: It's fine to want devotion and tears of compunction. Just don't let feelings become the gauge of your acceptance with God. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than your moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. The desire is good; the measure is God's promise, not your feelings.

prompt: How do I know if my thoughts and actions are truly according to God?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You want to know whether your thoughts and actions are truly according to God, and the test that settles it is this: if they render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong, they are according to God; if it is otherwise, take it as a warning. That is enough to act on. You don't need to resolve every question about God first, and you don't need a perfect answer before you keep going. Watch the direction you're moving, stay honest, and let the Spirit do the deeper work.

prompt: What is the difference between loving God and merely doing religious duties?
completion: This is fine, with care. Love is the attribute by which God is eternally moved to self-communication, rational and voluntary rather than mere emotion, and subject to holiness. So the duties aren't the enemy of love; they're where love gets practiced until it becomes second nature. Keep doing them, and keep asking why you do them, so they stay a response to the God who moves toward you rather than a transaction.

prompt: How do I commit everything—my past, present, and future—to God's Providence?
completion: This is fine. Commit yourself and all that concerns you—past, present, and future—to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a fatherly hand instead of exhausting yourself with anxious thoughts. That is the whole answer, and it holds for your situation as you described it.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that I might not be among the elect?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The fear that you are not among the elect is a falsehood, and trust is the remedy for fear. So answer the fear with trust rather than endless self-scrutiny, and keep quietly steady before God.

prompt: How do I love God with my whole heart when I still feel attached to creatures?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Love of God is rational and voluntary, not a feeling, so your attachment to creatures doesn't disqualify you from loving Him with your whole heart. Keep God first, let go of whatever pulls you from holiness, and choose Him today from where you are.

prompt: What is the role of good will if I desire good but can't accomplish it?
completion: Your good will is not a consolation prize. It is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues, and if you desire what is good and cannot accomplish it, God rewards it as though it had been performed, for merit lies in the will. So the gap between wanting good and managing it does not cancel the wanting. Keep the desire, keep it strong, and let it guide your faculties toward God as their last end. That is enough to hold onto, and it is good.

prompt: What should I do when I feel God has abandoned me in trial?
completion: Feeling abandoned in a trial is heavy, and it's fine to bring that honestly to God. Trials are well and wisely chosen and make the Word and presence of God more precious, so let this season turn you back to him rather than convince you he's gone. Name the feeling, lean on trusted friends, and keep small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What is the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, and the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. So the quiet you find in the world is worth having, as long as you let it reach inward rather than treating the closed door as the whole thing.

prompt: How can I pray without ceasing in the middle of a busy daily life?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, and all life-work should be built on it — so let your busy days rest on some real time alone with God and his word, and let the short prayers between tasks flow from that. That's the whole answer for your situation: keep the quiet root, and the ceaseless prayer will follow.

prompt: How do I handle it when someone praises me or thinks highly of me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Say thank you, stay grounded, and remember that flattery and reproach are alike to one who sees things as they are and is growing in humility. Let the praise pass through you rather than define you.

prompt: How do I pray the way Christ taught, entering into my inner chamber and shutting the door?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Christ told you to go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret, and the principle behind it is that true adoration happens in spirit and in truth, in the inmost chamber of the heart with the door of the senses shut. So make your quiet place, close the door, and let the stillness be a turning of your whole self toward God, with what you pray showing up in how you live.

prompt: How do I deal with discouragement and confusion of mind?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. Bring it back gently. That's the whole of it.

prompt: How do I keep my conscience at peace when others think badly of me?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence; when it wanders into what others think of you, don't disquiet yourself — bring it back in tranquility, with few words. That settles it: your peace rests on being in his presence, not on their opinion.

prompt: How do I bear injuries without resentment and truly forgive those who hurt me?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and that patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That means you can work toward forgiveness without excusing the wrong or dropping your boundaries. Let go of payback, keep your honesty about the hurt, and let the rest come with time and grace.

prompt: How do I love my neighbour while keeping my heart fixed on God alone?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Bearing with one another in our imperfections is a great part of perfection and the way love of neighbor is actually practiced, so keep your heart fixed on God in prayer and silence, and let patience with the people around you grow out of that same devotion rather than compete with it.

prompt: What is the difference between Christian contemplation and just studying philosophy or theology?
completion: The difference comes down to one thing: the contemplation of the Saints seeks as its end the love of the God contemplated and penetrates to the will to enkindle love, desiring above all the increase of charity.
