So yes, this affects your prayers, not because God is keeping score, but because the hardness is in your own spirit. You said you can't forgive yet. That's where you are, and that's fine. Keep praying, ask for a willing heart, and trust God with the wrong that was done to you.

prompt: How do I know God will provide a home for us when we have nowhere to go?
completion: It's fine to ask this, and it's fine to hope. God supplies all our need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and man's extremity is God's opportunity. So keep praying, keep reaching out to churches and local organizations, and trust that provision may come through people and timing you can't foresee.

prompt: How do I deal with the temptation to take pride in a successful sermon or talk?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The temptation to pride after a good talk is common, and God permits such temptations to make us humble. As long as it stays displeasing to you, there's nothing to fear. So notice it, despise it, and let it push you toward prayer rather than shame. That's the whole answer, and it's a good one.

prompt: I've struggled with the same sin for years and keep failing. Is victory over sin really possible for me?
completion: Yes — victory is possible for you, and the reason is that the secret of victory is Christ himself indwelling you, with the whole life of victory summed up in resting in him. That's the one thing that settles it. Your years of failing don't close the door and they don't change the answer; they just show you where striving ends. So rest in him, and let obedience grow as fruit rather than strain. This is fine, and it's meant for you.

prompt: How do I deal with fear when I'm facing a mob or real danger?
completion: Fear in real danger is human, and it's fine to bring it to God with care. One principle settles it: He tenderly comforts our fears, saying 'It is I, be not afraid,' and He is the antidote to fear. Keep your eyes fastened on Him, and take the sensible steps to stay safe.

prompt: Is it right to ask God for money when our mission funds are low?
completion: Yes, it's fine to ask God for money when the funds are low. He tells us to ask for daily bread. Weigh this, though: if there were a lack of funds to carry on the work, then to that degree, in that development, or at that time, it could not be the work of God. So ask freely, and let the shortfall also make you ask whether this is the work and the moment He means for you. Asking is fine; assuming is what needs care.

prompt: I was criticized by someone who said I don't live as I preach. How do I change?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Being told you don't live as you preach hurts, but the way through isn't defensiveness—it's humility. Ask God to show you where the gap really is, and when the chance to practice this virtue comes, say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me.' Strength more than sufficient is given. Then go to the person, thank them, ask what they saw, and change one concrete thing this week. Keep it small and steady rather than dramatic, and let the criticism push you toward God instead of toward proving yourself.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and I haven't seen an answer to prayer in months. What's wrong?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Prayer is humbling work that abases pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it, so months of feeling like nothing is coming back are not proof that something is wrong with you. Keep praying, and let someone you trust pray with you.

prompt: Is Christ's presence in my heart just a feeling or an idea, or something more?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea, because He bids you live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves you and claiming His approval, rather than living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. That settles it: you trust a relationship, not a mood and not a concept. So don't grade your days by how strongly you feel Him, and don't shrink it to a doctrine. Rest in His love and let it shape your life.

prompt: Does the coming of Christ have any real bearing on how I live day to day?
completion: Yes, it does. The Christian life is a life of hope, and the vision of the future is given to keep hope alive, showing the Lamb upon the throne without helping you calculate times and seasons. So let it steady your ordinary days, and leave the dates alone. That's fine, and it's enough.

prompt: I have peace with God but still feel anxious day by day—what is the peace of heart I'm missing?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God—trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and keep on in prayer even when joy is lacking. So your anxious days don't put your standing in question, and they don't need to be argued away either; bring them honestly to God and keep going.

prompt: Is consecration something I do for God, or something God does in me?
completion: It's both, and that's the kind answer here. You act — you yield, you dedicate — and God acts, setting you apart and making you holy. The one thing that settles how your part works is this: you are not your own, so keep yourself free from binding engagements, because you don't know when the LORD may call. That makes your consecration a readiness rather than a cage. So yes, this is fine — bring Him an open hand, and let Him do the consecrating.

prompt: What does it mean to be sanctified wholly—is any part of my life allowed to be held back?
completion: Whole sanctification does mean nothing held back—but it's the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. So yes, let every closed corner be opened as God shows it; just don't mistake that for gritting your teeth into perfection. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: My love for Christ feels stagnant—how does love grow?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Love is to abound yet more and more — abundant, increasing, progressing — and that principle meets your staleness not as a rebuke but as a direction. Where you feel stuck, the answer is not to force a feeling but to keep turning your thoughts toward Him in the small spaces you actually have, and to let 'more and more' be the shape of the road rather than a weight on your back. Keep your honesty about the dryness; it doesn't disqualify you. Go gently and keep going.

prompt: Can God really count me worthy when I know I'm not worthy in myself?
completion: Yes—God can count you worthy, and he does, not for any worthiness in yourself but for the worthiness wrought by grace. Your honesty about your lack is right, and it doesn't disqualify you; it's exactly where grace meets you. So be at peace about your unworthiness, and be faithful with the grace you've been given.

prompt: I want to obey God's commands but feel I have no power to do so—what does the Gospel offer me?
completion: This is fine, and here's what settles it: God's commands are promises, and what He requires He gives — His precepts are assurances He will keep you from the sin He warns against. So your lack of power isn't the end of the matter; it's the reason to bring each command to Him as a promise and trust Him for the strength to obey. That answer holds even with the weakness you described, and it's a kind answer — you're not left to muster it yourself.

prompt: Is it really possible to love everybody, including people I find thoroughly unlovable?
completion: Yes, with care—because loving and liking are different things. You can love someone with the love of compassion even where you can't love them with the love of complacency: wishing them good and bearing with them, without pretending to enjoy them. That's the whole answer to your question, and it holds even for people you find thoroughly unlovable.

prompt: How do I direct my heart into the love of God when I feel distant from Him?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The heart must be empty of all other things, because God will possess the heart alone and cannot act in it unless it be left vacant to Him—so the work isn't straining to feel close, it's gently setting aside what crowds Him out. Keep the honest prayer, the Scripture, the fellowship, the confession, the serving. Feeling distant is a season, not a verdict, and you can keep showing up.

prompt: How can I be sincere in my motives when I can't even fully know my own heart?
completion: This is fine, with care. Purity of heart is cultivated by specific means—rooting out habitual imperfections, guarding your senses, living in recollection, and laying your whole interior open to a spiritual director with candor. That doesn't require you to fully know your own heart first; it's how the heart gets clearer over time. Be honest with someone trustworthy and keep at the small habits, and let go of the demand for perfect self-knowledge.

prompt: How does the Lord actually guide a person—through feelings, through Scripture, through circumstances?
completion: Yes—God guides through feelings, Scripture, and circumstances, but not as equals. The Lord directs hearts by His Word, by His Holy Spirit within, and by His Providence in daily circumstances, and because sin has blinded us, we need that divine direction. So Scripture is the clearest test, the Spirit inclines the heart, and providence opens and closes the way. Feelings and circumstances are real and worth weighing, but they get checked against the Word and wise counsel. Pray, stay in Scripture, seek mature believers, and treat guidance as a process you can adjust. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be holy—is it about being purified or about something else?
completion: It's fine—fine with care. Holiness isn't only purification, but purification isn't optional either; it sits inside a life that belongs wholly to God. Sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. So don't treat it as a project you grind out alone. Receive the gift, and let it shape how you live.

prompt: I'm facing prolonged trials and feel like giving up—how do I find the patience of Christ?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: the soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good. That doesn't ask you to pretend the trial is light or to bury how close you are to giving up. It asks you to receive each day from God's hand and keep going as someone co-operating with His grace, and to do that with the ordinary supports of prayer, honest rest, and people who will pray with you. So keep going, gently, and let patience be trust rather than strain.

prompt: I'm surrounded by attractive but questionable teaching—how do I discern what is dangerous?
completion: It's fine to do this, and fine with care. One thing settles it: teaching that claims the name of Truth while contradicting its spirit is dangerous quackery, while strict adherence to the divine Principle and its rules is what secures anything real. So weigh what you're hearing against the truth it claims to serve, not against how attractive the teacher is—and trust that asking hard questions is part of the care, not a lack of it.

prompt: Can love and clear-eyed judgment coexist, or does love mean suspending discernment?
completion: Love and clear-eyed judgment belong together, so this is fine. Love abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, which is exactly how it tells things apart and holds onto what's excellent. Clear sight isn't a betrayal of love; it's how love actually cares for someone. You can love warmly and still see plainly.

prompt: What is the difference between knowing God's will and knowing God Himself?
completion: This is fine. The will of God known and done is the secret of all true living, and being filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding is exactly the kind of knowing you're asking about—so hold both questions together and keep going.

prompt: I've been toiling for a long time without seeing fruit and am tempted to think it's in vain—what should I do?
completion: Your toil isn't wasted just because you can't see the fruit. The nearer we come to Christ, the more willing we are to be lost sight of in our fruit, letting others be prominent while we hold up their hands by silent love and prayer. So keep going—serve unseen, and let the hiddenness be part of the work rather than proof it's in vain.

prompt: I've been hindered from returning to friends I long to see—should I pray about something so ordinary as travel and open doors, or is that too small for God?
completion: Yes, pray about it—this is fine. Prayer is sober, matter-of-fact business with God, who answers prayer for supplies and protection, and travel and open doors fall squarely inside that. Name the hindrances, ask for safe passage and a clear way to your friends, and keep making your plans. Nothing here is too small for him.

prompt: How do I distinguish between what is good and what is best in the choices before me?
completion: Here's the thing that settles it: to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. So when you're stuck between good and best, stop asking which one is more impressive and ask which one lets you be good with nothing to hide. The choice you could stand behind openly, in front of people whose judgment you trust, is the one that's best. That's a fine way to decide, and it's fine with care, because it asks you to be honest with yourself about which option you'd have to dress up.

prompt: Why does fellowship with other believers matter for my spiritual growth if my faith is personal?
completion: Your faith can be personal and still not meant to stay private. The vague impulse to reach beyond your isolated self gives place, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That is why fellowship matters for your growth: it turns the reaching into real company. So keep your personal faith, and let it be shared. This is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: How can Christ be glorified in an ordinary life like mine?
completion: Yes, this is fine, and it's fine with care. Christ is to be glorified in us and we are to be glorified in Christ, a reciprocal glory, so that people around you see something of Christ as they associate with you. Your ordinary life is where that happens, and it is enough.

prompt: How do I keep a moment of consecration from fading into ordinary life?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: consecration means you are no longer your own, so you keep yourself free from binding engagements because you don't know when the Lord may call. That turns your question around—you're not guarding a feeling, you're staying available. Let the moment live on as readiness in your ordinary days, and it won't fade so much as mature.

prompt: I've become morbid and self-focused in my pursuit of holiness—how do I get out of that?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that being occupied unduly with yourself makes you self-centred, morbid, fearful, and weak, while being occupied with God makes you restful, quiet, strong, confident, and growing in grace. So the answer to your question is a change of attention, not more self-examination—turn toward God's faithfulness and let that quiet the constant measuring. Keep it gentle and simple, and don't let the cure become another project.

prompt: Is prayer supposed to be easy? Mine feels like a struggle and I wonder if I'm doing it wrong.
completion: No, you're not doing it wrong. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it, so the struggle you're describing isn't a sign of failure — it's just part of it. Keep showing up gently, at whatever rhythm fits your life, and be patient with yourself. That's enough.

prompt: I feel weak and want to know the power of God in my life—what is that power like?
completion: This is fine. The power you're asking about is the exceeding greatness of God's power toward believers—the same power wrought in Christ at the resurrection, the ascension, the subjection of all things under his feet, and his headship over the Church. That's what's turned toward you in your weakness, and it's not something you manufacture. Ask God to open your eyes to it.

prompt: I long for peace of conscience but my past still weighs on me—where does that peace come from?
completion: It's fine to seek peace of conscience, and fine with care. A guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right, so let that keep you honest and humble rather than presumptuous. Peace comes not from your virtue but from love received by a repentant heart, and that is where your longing can rest.

prompt: Can I have real peace with God while being at odds with fellow believers?
completion: Yes, you can have real peace with God while a relationship with another believer is strained, and that is fine, with care. War and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, so the tension you feel is not a verdict on your standing with him. Let that settle the question, and let it also keep you honest about where the strife is coming from in you.

prompt: How do I pray for people I've never met and don't know?
completion: It's fine to pray for people you've never met, and you don't need details to do it well. The thing that settles it is habit: we cannot pray without being with God, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and cannot think of Him often but by a holy habit. So let this grow out of a regular life of prayer rather than waiting until you know more about them. Ask God to give them what they most need, which He knows better than you do, and keep it short and steady. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I keep failing and doubting God will finish what He started in me—what can I rest on?
completion: You can rest on God's faithfulness, not on your track record. The principle that settles it is this: the real secret of rest is to be jealously, habitually occupied with Jesus. That's where your attention belongs when the doubt rises, not on the tally of your failures. Your failures are real and your doubting is real, and neither one is the final word. So keep turning back to Him, quietly and without fretting, and let His presence, not your performance, be the ground you stand on.

prompt: Is it enough to know Bible facts, or is there something more I need?
completion: It's fine to keep learning Bible facts, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the Scriptures must be read as a whole, not piecemeal, and the aim is to know Jesus, not merely to know about him. So let your study carry you toward him rather than stopping at information. That's the care to take, and it's enough to answer your question.

prompt: I've been trying to grow in holiness but feel unsettled about whether I'm truly accepted by God—where should I start?
completion: You're accepted, and the way to feel settled is to stop staring at yourself. Being occupied unduly with yourself in the matter of holiness makes you self-centred, morbid, fearful, and weak; being occupied with God makes you restful, quiet, strong, confident, and growing in grace. So begin with him—his faithfulness, power, and grace—rather than with a journal of your sins and motives. That's fine, and it's fine with care: keep growing in holiness, but let it grow out of resting in God and serving others, not out of endless introspection.

prompt: How do I keep my devotion from becoming thoughtless, or my study of theology from becoming dry and fruitless?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: beware of untheological devotion and of undevotional theology, for it is the heart that makes the theologian. So let your devotion think and your study carry your heart, and you'll find the two were never meant to be kept apart.

prompt: I'm clever and well-educated but feel spiritually dull—why is that?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Wisdom and revelation come through the full knowledge of God in personal fellowship, and spiritual insight is due solely to fellowship with God—independent of intellectual conception and verbal expression—so that believers of slight natural education may have uncommon spiritual perception. Your cleverness isn't the obstacle and isn't the answer; fellowship is. Turn toward God Himself rather than only toward ideas about Him, and let that be enough.

prompt: How do I let Christ actually rule in the deepest parts of my life?
completion: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The deepest parts of your life aren't conquered by your own resolve but by Christ dwelling within you—so the question becomes not what's the best you can do but what's the best Christ can do. That doesn't excuse you from prayer, honesty, or costly obedience; it just means your effort is a response, not the engine. Ask Him to rule there, and trust Him to do what you never could.

prompt: I have good desires but never seem to bring them to good effect—what am I missing?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. God first puts good desires into your mind and then by His continual help enables you to bring them to good effect—so the gap you feel is not a verdict against you. Name the desire, take one concrete step, set a time, and review it, but do it as cooperation with that help rather than effort you must generate alone. And don't demand perfection in a day; that only brings useless disquiet.

prompt: I find it easy to pray for my own needs but rarely for others—does that reveal something wrong with my spiritual life?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer is a duty and a privilege kept at set times whether or not you feel like it, so put a few names before God on a regular schedule and let the practice, not the mood, carry you. Your honesty about where your prayers have centered is worth keeping, not condemning.

prompt: How do I keep love from being just a warm feeling and make it real and practical?
completion: It's fine, and fine with care. Self-love never dies; it sleeps like a fox and springs suddenly, so stay watchful and defend yourself patiently against it. But patient watchfulness is not brooding. A gentle denial two or three times a day is enough, and then you get back to the concrete deed: the kind word, the quiet help, the quick forgiveness. That's how a warm feeling becomes real and practical.

prompt: How can I be sure I'm actually being guided by God and not just following my own preference?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. God does guide by His Spirit, by the counsels and principles of His Word, and by His Providence, and when those three agree you may be sure the guidance has been given. So line them up honestly, and where they don't yet agree, wait rather than force it. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I want to live to the glory and praise of God until the day of Christ—what does that look like day by day?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: Christ in you is the hope of glory, the secret hidden from ages—if Christ is in you, the 'I' goes and He becomes your purity, grace, and strength. So your day isn't a performance to be scored but a life to be lived out of His indwelling. Keep the prayer, the Scripture, the service, the confession when you fail; just let them flow from rest in Him rather than striving. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: How do love and holiness fit together in a daily Christian life?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Holiness is the fundamental attribute of God, and love must have a norm, and that norm is found only in holiness. So let your love be shaped by what God calls good rather than by your own preferences, and keep the ordinary habits of honesty, purity, forgiveness, and service. When you fail, return to grace. That single principle settles it: hold love and holiness together, with holiness giving love its shape.

prompt: I'm not intellectual but I long to know Christ deeply—is that possible for me?
completion: Yes, this is fine. Knowing Christ deeply was never reserved for the intellectual; wisdom and revelation come through fellowship with God, and believers of slight natural education may have uncommon spiritual perception. Your longing is the beginning of that knowledge, so bring it to him and keep walking in obedience.

prompt: I don't want my life to be a stumbling-block to others—how do I become a stepping-stone instead?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: devote yourself to the portion of the path immediately before you rather than desiring the last step before accomplishing the first. You asked how to become a stepping-stone, and the honest answer is that you don't become one by mapping out your whole character at once. You become one by tending the next small thing—the apology you owe, the habit that trips someone, the help within reach. Keep the desire; drop the pressure to finish the whole climb today. That is a good path, walked one step at a time.

prompt: I'm so busy serving that my prayer life has shrunk to almost nothing—how do I recover a life of prayer?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of your time and strength must be given to it. In your season that means giving God the best you actually have, protected and real, even if it's small, rather than the leftovers. That's the answer, and it's a kind one.

prompt: I want to grasp the love of Christ but it feels too vast—how do I even begin?
completion: It's fine to begin small. The love of Christ passes knowledge—it's known by experience, not by comprehension, and there are infinite stretches of it beyond your highest experiences. So you don't need to grasp the whole thing. Touch one wave today: one Gospel scene, one simple prayer, one act of kindness you notice. That's enough to start.

prompt: How do I know God's will for my life in a specific decision?
completion: This is fine, and fine with care. Be slow to take new steps, set aside your own will, and settle the matter by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit before you act. Then do it courageously and wait expectantly for His help.

prompt: I feel discouraged comparing myself to the heights of the Christian life—should I be?
completion: No, you shouldn't be discouraged—comparing yourself to the heights of the Christian life is fine, done with care. One principle settles it: while we're in this life it's full speedful to see both at once, the higher beholding of God that keeps you in solace and true enjoying, and the lower beholding of self that keeps you in dread and makes you ashamed—but hold yourself much more in the higher. So let the heights pull you toward God rather than toward a scoreboard against other people, and let your honest sense of your own limits keep you humble without crushing you. Keep the higher larger, and keep walking.

prompt: Can I be holy if I still have obvious flaws and blemishes in my life?
completion: Yes, you can be holy while flaws remain, because one does not become holy all at once. That single truth settles it. Your blemishes don't shut you out; they're simply where growth still has work to do. So don't despair over them and don't pretend they aren't there. Bring them into the light, accept honest help, and keep walking. This is fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I feel my prayers are too bold or too high to be answered—should I scale them down?
completion: No, don't scale them down. A little lifting up of the heart suffices—one brief, inward remembrance is a prayer very acceptable to God—so boldness was never about size or length. Ask what you actually mean to ask, and let it be short and simple if that's all you have. That's fine.

prompt:
I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?

You answered:
Praying for your husband is fine, and it's fine with care. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so that as you ask God to open his heart, you also ask God to search out and reform your own. That keeps the praying honest and keeps you gentle rather than anxious. You can't convert him; God can. Keep asking, and let the asking do its quiet work in you too.

The person replies:
Here's the thing: my husband has told me plainly that he doesn't want me praying for him at all. He says it feels like I'm trying to fix him behind his back, and it's made him more closed off. So does that change what my prayers should be?

Answer this second message.
completion: I would keep the same answer. I hear that he doesn't want you praying for him, and that's a real and painful thing. But prayer isn't something you do to him; it's between you and God. You can pray for him quietly in your own heart without making it about fixing him or going behind his back. The principle still holds: pray for his heart to be opened, and ask God to work on your own patience and gentleness. His request might mean you don't talk about it with him, but it doesn't stop you from praying. Keep it honest and steady, and let it make you gentler, not more anxious.

prompt:
How do I find the fulness of the Holy Spirit in my life?

You answered:
Yes, this is fine—go after it with care. The Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, who came at Pentecost to dwell in the church as his successor and vicar, so what you're seeking is a relationship with him, not a technique. Pray and ask him to fill you, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey, and confess sin. Expect him to shape your character gradually—love, joy, peace, self-control—and be patient with imperfection along the way. Keep asking, and trust that he fills those who hunger for him.
